subtopic: MR. ROSS (MOOSE JAW)-CBC NEWS BROADCAST RESPECTING WAR APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: On a matter of privilege, Mr. Speaker, last evening at ten o'clock the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation carried a news item to the effect that the war appropriation bill had been given first and second readings in this house while less than twenty-five members were present in the chamber. I was present at that time, Mr. Speaker, and that statement is incorrect. There were many more than twenty-five members in this chamber at that time. In giving news reports in regard to this House of Commons, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and all others who distribute news throughout this country should be very careful to give correct reports. Whoever prepared "that report should have known that an ;important ceremony was taking place in front of these buildings at which His Excellency the Governor General was present; that on the platform with His Excellency were the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, several of the cabinet ministers and many [DOT] members of the House of Commons, and that it would have been a matter of discourtesy for them to leave the scene before His Excellency left. I believe a report of that kind should be corrected, and that those responsible for such reports should be reprimanded by what-'ever minister of this government has the right to reprimand the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, June 8, consideration in committee of Bill No. 95, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
On section 2-Appropriation $2,000,000,000 less $500,000,000 voted under 1942 c.9.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with my limitations in the English language it might have been better if I had addressed the committee in my maternal tongue, but in order that all hon. members may follow what I have to say I shall try to express myself in English. I should like to offer a few short comments under this bill which provides $2,000,000,000 for the defence, security and welfare of Canada. For the benefit of the members of the war cabinet may I recall what I said in this house on May 6, 1941, with regard to oil possibilities in the Gaspe district. I quote from page 2822 of Hansard of that date:
I have already referred to the possibilities of oil bearing areas in the Gaspe bay surroundings. From 1860 up to 1901, with rudimentary machinery, fifty wells have been drilled at a relatively small depth. One can read with profit and interest the records on each of these drillings and their oil output in the annual report of the Quebec bureau of mines for 1929 by Mr. William A. Sparks. Oil occurrences can be found to-day on the surface of the soil in many places over an area of six hundred square miles. In his 1929 report, Mr. William Sparks writes this on page 7:
"The occurrence of oil in small quantity has been fully established, with the result that the district has continued to attract attention and it must still be regarded as ; a possible source of oil on a commercial scale."
And here is what we read in a recent report by the joint engineers. Doctor I. W. Jones and Mr. H. W. McGerrigle, for the year 1937 at pages 36 and 37:
"There is some oil of good quality in this region, as has long been known. . . . _ The region is recommended to the serious consideration of those in search for oil."
By reason of the imperative necessity imposed by actual events of attempting to discover new sources of oil, and, by recalling the past policy of Great Britain in investing large capital to develop oil wells in Roumania, Iraq and many other well known countries, I deem it is the government's duty to undertake forthwith the drilling of such areas in Gaspe as are recommended by these engineers.
According to quotations I have lately received from Robert McMaster and Sons, of Onondaga, Ontario, the drilling of a 7,000 foot well-the probable oil bearing depth

could be undertaken at a cost of $78,000. The investment of $500,000 would then permit the drilling of seven wells which could be concurrently done

Wor Appropriation
and completed in eight months time to supply, thereafter, at Gaspe seaport, the navy and the air force, with oil which at that time might have become scarce elsewhere.
As a matter of fact I believe oil has become quite scarce since that time. On many occasions since last May I have tried to call to the attention of the government the necessity of making some search for oil in that region. I turn now to sessional paper No. 140, in which appear certain questions and replies in connection with this matter. The following question appeared in issue No. 21 of Votes and Proceedings:
1.	In view of recent military developments, has the government given any consideration to the fuel oil problem?
2.	If so, what consideration has been given to the possibilities of exploiting the petroleum deposits of Gaspe?
To these questions the following answer was given by Mr. G. K. Sheils, deputy minister:
2. No special geological or geophysical work has been done in the Gaspe peninsula of recent date. The reports on record, which are reasonably complete, and the drilling which was carried on, are not encouraging for large production of oil. It has been deemed advisable to give first attention to other areas in Canada which give better promise.
Following this answer, which was published in the press, I received some letters from oil experts, men well acquainted with the oil possibilities of Gaspe. The following is a letter from Mr. L. J. McKenzie of Gaspe, Quebec, addressed to the editor of the Herald. This letter, published in the latter part of January, 1942, is as follows:
To the Editor of the Herald:
Sir,-There is much of vital public interest in a recent article in your paper "Minerals to Win the War"-extracts from Mr. Claud M. Johnston's letter.
In the course of his letter Mr. Johnston mentions the lead and zinc possibilities of the Gaspe peninsula, but he appears to have overlooked Gaspe's petroleum possibilities.
In these most critical times when democracy is fighting for her very life and future existence. on oil and for oil, it seems to us that our leaders should be brought to realize more fully the necessity of an unstinted, all-out effort towards the proper drilling and thorough testing of the Gaspe oil-bearing strata.
Canada now imports practically all the petroleum she uses, and here we have a proven oil prospect of 250 square miles, situated at the mouth of the St. Lawrence; 300 miles nearer Europe than any other point in America (Labrador excepted), with petroleum seeping out of the rocks in dozens of places from the very shores of the gulf to thirty miles inland, and not one really serious effort being made towards determining what quantity exists at depth. Opposed interests must not be considered, and, as Mr. Johnston says, "there is a way to find out."
It does not take an over-vivid imagination to picture what petroleum in quantities here at the mouth of the St. Lawrence would mean to our dominion and our allies.
I will not go into details of our reasons for confidence in the prospect more than to say that I have personally seen one well flow thousands of barrels in this region, and I am convinced.
Yes we have iron ore, copper and other base metals for the building of ships and planes and we believe we also have the oil to propel those ships and fly the planes as well.
Following the publication in the press of the answers tabled in the house in February I received the following letter from an oil expert associated with Cecil Carpenter and Company, Limited:
I read with much interest your remarks at Ottawa regarding the last drilling results for oil in Gaspe. . . . My name as identified with the past exploration for oil in Gaspe possibly may not be known to you. I lived in Gaspe for many years operating as general manager of the Petroleum Oil Trust of London, England; subsequently manager for other companies operating there. At the closing of these operations I promoted, organized and built the A.Q. and W. Railway, now the Canadian National, from New Carlisle to Gaspe harbour.
The New Canadian Company Limited held the construction contract for the railway of which I was the managing director. Under these circumstances I have been much interested in the latest exploration to try for oil in quantity.
My oil companies retained excellent oil experts, both Russian and French; likewise the late Mr. Obalski, Quebec government engineer, kept in close touch with developments. It does not appear feasible that oil should be found in 80 per cent of my wells drilled and the stratification refuse to produce more. The consensus of opinion then was that once we could increase the width of porous strata we were on the road to success.
The letter concludes with this paragraph:
I would always be pleased to cooperate with you for the betterment and development of any enterprise in Gaspesia, because I put in so many years there and think the people in that country are the best in Canada.
C. B. K. Carpenter
Then, I received another interesting letter, dated at Hawkesbury, Ontario, March 2, 1942, as follows:
Dear Sir:
According to a press report before me, a report on the production of oil in the Gaspe peninsula has been tabled in the House of Commons.
I wish to say I have been and still am in the position of investigator of fraudulent work carried on to suppress the oils of Canada. I have been so for twenty-one years, not employed by any firm, group or government. I was requested by the British government through their British trade commission to take up the work in 1922, and found it so interesting that after taking five years in geology and field work I continued at my own expense.
War Appropriation

There is no reason why one dollar's worth of oil should be brought into Canada, if such fraudulent work were suppressed by the government; and now in our war effort surely something can be done.
An early reply will be appreciated, and I may add that I may this year spend a month in your district if time permits.
This letter is signed by Mr. A. C. McIntosh, Box 145, Hawkesbury.
Yesterday I asked the government if it was the intention to give some thought to the possibilities of oil production in Gaspe, in view of the fact that the oil and fuel problem is becoming so acute. We all know that the shortage of oil and gasoline seriously affect the whole of our population, and bring upon us many difficulties.
May I draw to the attention of the committee a further consequence of gasoline rationing. I have no doubt all hon. members have heard about Gaspesia-its beautiful scenery, its boundless sea, its vast mountains, its wide rivers, and its delicious fish. In past years Gaspe has been known as one of the most beautiful spots in Canada, and its beauties have been a strong inducement to tourists. The tourist traffic in that part of Canada has been a source of revenue from which the whole of the dominion has benefited. Under a system of rationing of gasoline however it will not be possible for the duration of the war to travel extensively through Gaspe.
There is a fine chain of hotels along the coast which provides very good accommodation for tourists. There is no railroad on the north side of the Gaspe peninsula and if we are unable to get gasoline these hotel owners will fail. There is nothing else to support them but the tourist trade. The tourist industry is very important to Canada. This bill is to provide for the defence and welfare of Canada and also for the payment of indemnity to those who suffer war damages. If the government are not willing to ease the gas restrictions for a month or two to permit tourists to come into this country, perhaps they would be willing to pay an indemnity to these hotel owners. I think something should be done, particularly in view of the fact that provision has been made for other classes of industry in Canada in the matter of war damage.
There are great possibilities on the Gaspe coast for assistance to our war effort. I have mentioned the metals that are to be found there. There are three mining companies which own properties on the Gaspe peninsula. Some thirty-five or forty miles from Ste. Anne des Monts the Federal Zinc Mining

company have properties from which they extract hundreds of tons of zinc and lead. These metals are lying there because of lack of transportation facilities. We are facing a shortage of metals and I think the government should do something to exploit these mines and permit the movement of these metals. The mountains of the Gaspe peninsula are covered with all types of hardwoods which could be used to build ships. There is a shortage of shipping in Canada and there are a number of fine inlets along the coast where skilled labour is available for the construction of wooden ships from one hundred tons to five hundred tons in size. I think the government should consider this proposition.
Another matter which should be considered in connection with this bill is the lack of transportation facilities to take the fish produced in the Magdalen islands to the West Indies and south American ports. The main production is smoked herring and salt mackerel. These fish are not suitable for home consumption and if they are to be sold it is necessary that they be transported to these foreign ports. The fish exporters in Halifax say that they will not be able to move this fish this fall because of a shortage of vessels. The Minister of Fisheries told me a few days ago that it was quite certain that ships could not be obtained for the transporting of this fish. If these fishermen are unable to sell their product they will have nothing to take them through the winter. This bill provides for the payment of indemnities to those suffering from war damages, and I think the government should take immediate steps to either provide ships or to pay indemnities to these producers.
A word or two as to the defence of Canada. If Canada is threatened, if there is a chance of our being conquered, we should take every possible step to save ourselves from attack. Much has been said about the defence of the Atlantic coast. Halifax is situated close to that entrance formed by Newfoundland on the one side and Cape Breton island on the other. There is no doubt that Halifax is in the attack zone, but the Gaspe coast and the St. Lawrence river provide the real entrance to Canada and they are inside this barrier. Engineers have said that from the defence point of view Gaspe harbour is most important to Canada. There are some defence works there but they are not adequate to protect the Gaspe coast and the St. Lawrence. Hon. members will recall that only a short time ago two ships were sunk in the St. Lawrence. One was sunk

War Appropriation
almost 250 miles above Gaspe, which is nearly half way between Gaspe cape and Montreal. The other one was a little further down the river. These torpedoings show the dangers of attack.
At Mont Joli, some ten miles below Rimouski, there is an air training school, but there are almost 250 miles of coast which are absolutely unprotected. The north shore of the St. Lawrence has no defence of any kind; there are no guns and there are no soldiers. Along that route to Quebec, Montreal and the upper lakes there is no defence at all until you get to Quebec. Some of the money provided by this bill could be used to good advantage in providing some defence works down there.
Perhaps if more ships were sunk it would be realized that the facilities of Gaspe should be properly organized. We should be able to take care of these ships that are damaged. There is no dry dock in that part of the country and there are only a few guns and defence works. That is not enough to prevent the Germans from attacking. I take advantage of this opportunity to offer my thanks to the government and congratulate them upon what has been done so far, but it is not sufficient. We want and we need more defence in case of attack. If there is no danger at all of attack, and no danger of losing our country, we do not need any defence; but if there is danger we need the proper defence works, and it is time to provide them.
I would ask the Minister of National Defence or any other of the ministers concerned if they would assure the committee that something will be done to develop the oil resources of Gaspe and to take advantage of our ability to build ships. The material is right there. All it needs is proper organization and communications to develop these resources. We have proven mines there of lead and zinc. What is the government going to do about these things? What is the government going to do about the tourist traffic, which is hampered by gas rationing? What is the government going to do for better defence of the St. Lawrence?

I wish to say a few words about the wages paid in war industry in the county of Shefford. I am afraid that the war plants in my constituency are paying the smallest wages of any war plants in Canada. I am sure that the wages paid there are much lower than the wages paid, for example, at Valleyfield, Bouchard and Cherrier. It will be remembered that an explosion occurred at one of these war plants in my constituency, resulting in the deaths of six or eight persons.
Some time ago I asked a question in the house as to the scale of wages paid but, as often happens, I received a negative answer. It was to the effect that they were paying the average rate of wages paid in the locality. I maintain that there should be a uniform scale of wages in all war plants, throughout the same province at least. I would not expect the government to pay as high wages in war plants as they are paying in the shipbuilding industry in Vancouver, where the rate I understand is around $1 an hour. But certainly female labour should be remunerated in munitions plants at a higher rate than 25 to 27 cents an hour, and men at a higher rate than 35 cents an hour.
A lot of small munitions plants are to be started in Granby, and I hope that before they get started the government will see that the employees are paid a fair wage. I am asking the government to see that these employees get paid as much as employees of other war plants in the province of Quebec. I am sorry to say that in my own community, the city of Granby, the wages are not as high as they should be. I am told-I do not know whether it is correct or not-that some men who hold high positions in the town of Granby used their influence to prevent a new industry from paying higher wages. I do know that we have some sweat shops where female labour is paid 15 cents an hour, and while this is not perhaps a federal government matter I want to impress upon the government, which has control of munitions plants, the importance of paying a fair and reasonable wage. The Minister of Labour may say: We do not want to interfere with the labour laws of the province. But I can assure him and this government that if you pay labour 10 cents an hour more than the provincial scale of wages there will be no reproaches from anybody.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should
like to deal with a matter which has not been taken up yet, but is under this bill, and it is one of the most important matters of all, being related to external affairs. Never since the war started have we had an adequate opportunity to discuss this department or its functions or even Canada's foreign policy- because Canada has never yet had a foreign policy. I should like to say a few words on external affairs in connection with this item on page 2921 of Hansard showing a total of $456,000 for external affairs, divided as follows:	Administration and passport office,
$265,000; representation abroad, $100,000- our representatives in Japan, Holland, Belgium, France and one or two other places have been washed out; consular services, $5,500; evacuation of staff from abroad, $5,000; Canada-United States permanent joint board on defence-very largely board and very little defence-$22,500; Canadian section of joint economic committee, $53,000-a total, Mr. 
Chairman, under one department of civil estimates of $456,000, and we have no adequate details as to how it is made up or anything about it.
I can tell you this:	in time of war these
separate Canadian legations and representations abroad have caused Britain's influence to be divided. They are bad enough during peace, let alone in war, and some of them have had a purely mischievous effect so far as defence and foreign affairs are concerned.
Canada has never yet had a foreign policy. No one can tell what it is-it is negative. At the last imperial conference, in 1937, when we knew of the danger to the empire, and Australia specifically pointed out the grave conditions in the Pacific, Canada took the position, "We have no commitments; parliament will decide," and things remained that way until war was declared. We would not even take part in or aid an empire shipbuilding policy at that 1937 conference.
I wish again, to raise this matter of an empire war cabinet. It is the most important thing that we can consider at the present time. The coordination of the efforts of the dominions is the most important duty of the hour. The peril is at the gate, and it is possible that three of the dominions, namely Australia, New Zealand, and south Africa, will be invaded. One of the northern islands of Australia has already been invaded, and New Zealand is in grave danger. Both of these fine dominions have had to appeal to the United States. The supremacy of the Pacific has been lost, and Japan is moving around the Pacific like a circus through 15,000 miles of islands, menacing the coasts of Madagascar, the islands of the Indian ocean and the very eastern shores of south Africa, in the Indian ocean, where the prime minister of the union, General Smuts, has appealed for support to the very native races from whom his people took the franchise in 1854.
As I have said, Australia pointed out over a year ago the dangers which threatened her in the far east, and asked the British government to reestablish the empire war cabinet. During the last war this cabinet functioned. It consisted of the prime ministers of the five dominions, New Zealand, Australia, South Africa, Canada and Newfoundland. Our Prime Minister remarked one day recently in this chamber that he could not attend such a conference or support such a war cabinet, and that it was not necessary.
During the last war a war cabinet did wonderful work to win the war. The principle was established that the Prime Minister or his dominion representative could be there. For example, the late General Botha, when

War Appropriation
prime minister of South Africa, nominated as his representative Lieutenant-General Smuts, now Field Marshal Smuts, the present premier of the union. The empire war cabinet did a great deal of good, increased dominion aid wonderfully and to its absence must be attributed many of the unhappy conditions which have developed in the far east in the last two years. Right Hon. Robert Menzies, the able statesman who, when prime minister of Australia, addressed this house last fall, and the present prime minister, Mr. Curtin, have referred to the absence of coordination, especially in the domain of joint policy in the far east, and the great need of an empire war cabinet. Recently they have complained that decisions have been made adverse to their interests without consultation with the Australasian or other dominions. Unless there is a war cabinet-which Canada, for some reason has opposed-there can be no joint consultation or cooperation or united action by the dominions in the present war. It is too bad that Canada has taken this stand, because our country is dependent on the mother country in this war as she was in the last for all our protection from invasion. It is a grave responsibility to refuse a war cabinet.
In view of the loss of the command of the sea in the Pacific, the disaster at Pearl Harbour, and the fall of Singapore, Hong Kong, Malaya and Burma and other strongholds, the need of an imperial war cabinet was never more apparent than now. It is a tragedy which will soon be costly to Canada. Since the Victorian era the imperial conference system has been a useful method of communication and consultation between the dominions and the mother country. The first colonial conference took place in 1887 and was continued every five years. Conferences have been held periodically, as in 1907, 1917, 1937 and other times. There were memorable meetings-at the time of the diamond jubilee of Queen Victoria, in 1897, following the accession of King Edward VII, in the closing years of the war, and at the time of the coronation of our present king in 1937. Although these assemblies have no legislative powers, they are valuable in peace time as a means of expression of the views of the dominions concerning imperial policies. They are even more necessary in time of war, because of the vastness of our empire and its manifold relations with foreign states. I have urged this matter repeatedly upon the government since the war started. It is discouraging to see this separatist stand taken and the plea of Australia ignored and our sister dominions, 44561-201
Australia and New Zealand have been, as a result, compelled to appeal for help to the United States. The help which our United States friends have given has been magnificent. True it is that the United States has been able as yet to provide only about 50 per cent of her expected allotment for 1942 to Russia and Great Britain or to Australia, but the will is there, and before six months is over this provision will have been greatly increased.
I raised this subject of the relationship of the dominions to Great Britain in connection with empire day, on the 22nd of last month. It was surprising to me that on a day like that, remembering all that we owe to the mother country in this war because she bore the whole brunt of it for two years alone, that this parliament did not see fit to say anything about it as I suggested on empire day or Victoria day, and to pay her tribute and thanks. Hon. Walter Nash, the very able minister of New Zealand, who addressed us recently, paid a great tribute to the old country. He said:
That little spot called Britain, when we understand what she has done, though some of what she has done have been mistakes, we must see that she has on the credit side an amazing balance. We are out to help her win because we want her to win. Unless the old country wins all that we cherish will disappear.
The non-cooperative attitude of Canada has been criticized elsewhere than in this country. That well known publisher and empire builder, the very able Sir Keith Murdoch, who owns a number of newspapers in Australia, including the Melbourne Herald, referring to the situation in the far east, remarked that not only our difficulties there and the trouble in the far east but also the fact that we have a war at all, must be largely attributed to the fact that the empire not only threw away her defences on land, sea and in the air, but threw away her friends as well. In a letter, urging a war cabinet, to the London Times after the disaster at Pearl Harbour, he stated:
. . . The entry of stout dominion minds into the war council, and of oversea service men and business men into the army, navy, air and supply councils has become of great importance for the two reasons that the dominions will not stand grave decisions going against them unless they are in those decisions, and that something must be done to improve the war management. . . .
He went on to criticize the weaknesses of our fighting services and emphasized lack of coordination as largely responsible for the disasters which have befallen us in the far east.
Mr. Menzies, the former prime minister of Australia who addressed this house, Mr. Chairman, from where you are sitting, stated that

War Appropriation

he had known for a long time of the inadequacy of the empire's defences in the Pacific, and that they revealed a very dangerous condition of weakness. These views are practically identical with those expressed by Prime Minister Fraser of New Zealand and by Mr. Curtin, successor to Mr. Menzies as Prime Minister of Australia, and it is charged in England and Australia that Canada knew all about it also and did nothing about it, and in none of these dominions were the people aware of the danger, or the facts disclosed.
The empire is worth fighting for in this emergency, because if it passes, freedom and liberty and civilization and religion will vanish from the earth. But for the glorious stand of the mother country after Dunkirk we on this continent, including the United States, would long ago have had to seek peace with the axis powers. It was a very grave mistake for our country, when asked by Mr. Churchill what our views were, to give the refusal we did. The two decades between 1918 and 1939 were the most disastrous years in the whole history of the world. Canada did not show up any too well in the discussion at the imperial conference in 1937 although Canada was one of the world's chief traders. We had no foreign policy; this external affairs vote showed that. The two decades I named above were full of mistakes and errors since the last war, and now this war threatens the freedom and liberty and religion of the world, and if we do not bestir ourselves it means the end also of civilization. It is too bad that we keep up in the clouds, dreaming yet about isolation and status. The upheaval brought about by this war was not occasioned by anything that happened before 1918. It arose out of what happened since, largely out of the desire for greater prosperity, and reliance on peace pacts and agreements, Kellogg pacts, Locarno, the status quo, the Monroe doctrine, and collective security-which is only security when we have an armed Britain. That is one of the reasons for this disastrous condition. We have forgotten to listen to the lessons of experience and history, namely, in peace to prepare for what may come after. Without a war cabinet we see the result in Hong Kong and Singapore. Most important matters have been settled and given against us, and we have not been consulted or had a word to say about it.
To-day is the eighty-second day of this session, and we have not had one word since we started on estimates on foreign affairs outside of the Prime Minister's statement last year about two or three new embassies. This country was the chief drifter from the British
tMr. Church.]
empire before the war started. It is bad enough in peace time to have this drifting, but in war time it is fatal. Three of the dominions are on the border of disaster. If we lose, they may not belong to the empire much longer; they have had to appeal to the United States for help. While our neighbours to the south are a great people, they were not a military power at the start, and for a couple of years they cannot do a great deal to help in the present struggle because it will take two years to be fully armed. With the enemy at the front door and the back door and the side door and every other door, we have to get on with the total war for which the people voted on April 27.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Before this important bill passes I desire to refer to a matter which I regard as of supreme importance. I have not in the last six weeks troubled the house by occupying any time in the discussion of this measure, and I make no apology for bringing to the attention of the committee and the government the matter with which I shall now deal very briefly.
I quote from section 2 of the bill, paragraphs (a) and (d):
(a) the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada;
(d) The earying out of any measure deemed necessary or advisable by the governor in council in consequence of the existence of a state of war.
In this connection I suggest to the government that it is of immediate and major importance that at least three strategic points in Canada should be protected with barrage balloons. I am not making this appeal without having submitted my views to the authorities, who I thought should first have them brought to their attention; and among those authorities is our division of the joint defence board. I found on their part no sympathy concerning the matters that I brought forward. Notwithstanding that, and notwithstanding the lapse of some time, I wish it to be understood that I make these suggestions in an absolutely constructive and friendly spirit and not as a critic.
I had the privilege, with five associates in this house, of visiting the mother country a few short months ago. Portsmouth, Liverpool, Glasgow, Hull, Newcastle-every important port in the British empire was provided with thorough and efficient barrage balloon protection. Men in the air force over there told me that they feared nothing so much in an attack upon enemy objectives across the channel as to be obliged to attempt to dive-bomb any objective which was protected by barrage balloons. They extend to between

War Appropriation
3,000 and 4,000 feet in height, entirely surrounding a port or city or war plant, and any enemy dive-bomber seeking to come within that area and get within 4,000 feet of his objective might just as well sign on with the suicide squad before attempting it. They are the greatest means of protection to-day.
Halifax has no barrage balloon protection. Esquimalt, the only dry dock under the control of the British empire on the Pacific ocean, has no barrage balloon protection. Patricia Bay, the great airport on the Pacific coast, has no barrage balloon protection. Halifax is a tinder town in this respect; it has a great many inflammable wooden build* ings, which are so susceptible to incendiary bombs that the very thought of it almost makes one shudder. Ammunition dumps are located there, as well as docks for the repair of vessels. We all know- it is the centre for the convoys which are made up to go to the motherland. The destruction of Liverpool tomorrow morning would not be as great a blow at the British empire, to say nothing of Canada, as any enemy action would be which would make a rubble heap of Halifax. There is no port, no strategic war industry on the whole north American continent the destruction of which would mean such a terrific loss to the British empire and the united nations as the destruction of Halifax overnight would mean to our war effort.
Some one may say: "Don't be an alarmist; it can't happen here." That phrase is long outmoded. If an enemy aeroplane carrier crept up under favourable weather conditions, fog and so forth, within 100 miles of Halifax, and released thirty or forty bombers which could drop incendiary and explosive bombs on Halifax, I hate to think what the result might be.
Now that we are appropriating $2,000,000,000 for national defence and security I make this suggestion in all seriousness to the government, to the authorities, to the joint defence board for north America. I feel sure that the United States members of that board, if asked what one spot in north America we could least spare, would be bound to say without a dissenting voice, the city of Halifax. I am making no appeal for the protection of the residents of that city. They are a game people. They are willing to take all the chances that war imposes upon them. But even leaving that aside, from the empire standpoint; from the standpoint of the war effort; from every standpoint from which a reasonable man who will examine the subject as I have examined it can reach a conclusion, I do suggest that we must at once provide barrage balloon protection for Halifax, Esquimalt and Patricia Bay.

speechtext:
I am interested in the subject matter brought up by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), and I have wondered why the suggestion was not made before. One reason why I have not made it previously was this. I too had the honour of visiting Britain last year, when I had a long discussion with the commander of the Dover area, as well as with officers at Portsmouth, with respect to this subject of barrage balloons. During the course of a tour down the Thames, covering a good many miles, we saw a long line of barrage balloons protecting that area. I questioned the officers with respect to both the expediency and the desirability of having this system of barrage balloons over strategic points. On balance they advocated their retention, but I was told some very curious stories. One officer told me that when the balloons were first installed over Dover the Germans were greatly intrigued. They would come over each morning and shoot down the balloons just about as soon as they were raised; when they were raised again they would come back and shoot them down again, and this happened on a number of occasions. Of course the balloons are very vulnerable and can be punctured by a bullet. After that the Germans left them alone, but the British are still of the opinion that these balloons form a valuable auxiliary to the defence of a given position. That is so for the very reason that has been explained to this committee by the hon. member for Parry Sound, namely, that they are a deterrent to dive bombing, and prevent those operating by air against a given point from coming too close. That is why they are being retained. I assume that our general staff, our defence officials, studied this position long ago, and it does seem to me they might state their opinion with respect to a port like Halifax, which I suppose is the most vulnerable of all.
Just in passing, I have often wondered why there should be so much concentration at Halifax. There are a great many important works for which there is not very much defence. I do not think the hon. member need apologize or give any excuse for raising this question. It is a matter of importance in the defence of some of the vulnerable places in Canada, and I commend his remarks to the Minister of National Defence.

Much as I should like to see the discussion of labour problems proceed, and much as I am interested in the question raised by the hon. member for Parry Sound, yet I do think that before our discussion goes too far afield, following the discussion we had on the night of June 5, I
31 SO
War Appropriation

should direct the attention of the committee once more to the all-important question of inflation, and how inflation might reasonably be met and guarded against. There is no more important question facing the peoples of the British empire and the United States to-day than the question of inflation, and I venture to say there is no question which is less understood. In my brief and limited experience there is no question less understood than the all-important question of money, yet there is nothing which has come closer to causing war, both international and civil, than that question. So if hon. members of the committee will bear with me, I will revert to the matter we were discussing on Friday afternoon.
The Minister of Finance was kind enough to make some remarks which I thought indicated a great deal of progressiveness on his part. I should like to read to the committee several of his statements, and I should like the minister to elaborate on those statements a little more fully so that I may see just how nearly I can come to agreeing with him. I turn first to page 3110 of Hansard, where I find this statement:
Mr. Ilsley: If the Social Credit party is not against borrowing and is not against taxing and is not against private ownership, then the difference between the Social Credit party and the government comes down to this, just a difference in judgment as to how much money should be issued from time to time.
I was startled when the minister made that remark, because I had been led to suspect that he was much further removed from us than his words indicated. Now, before beginning to develop my subject, may I just comment briefly on that passage. We were discussing the question of war financing; and let me fepeat that social credit does believe that it is necessary to tax during war. Ordinarily the attitude of social credit toward taxation is this, that for the major portion of the population it is not good to tax. Generally there is a shortage of purchasing power which renders the people unable to buy the goods which industry is able to produce. Consequently any measure which will decrease that purchasing power tends to aggravate the evil from which the community in modern times suffers, namely inadequate buying power. In time of war, however, we realize that in order to withdraw some of the surplus purchasing power which might embarrass the government by causing too great a buying pressure, it is necessary to use taxation discreetly.
With respect to borrowing, our general attitude is this, that it is inadvisable for a government to borrow. We believe that the bane of existence of the modern state is debt. We believe that debt should be guarded against

by every means at the disposal of an administration. Yet again we grant that in time of war a measure of borrowing is necessary.
Now with respect to the private ownership of industry, it is an essential characteristic of the social credit concept, as opposed to the socialistic concept, that industry will be much better taken care of, it will be much more efficient, the people engaged in industry will be much happier, and the state will be much more democratic if individuals own the industries. We therefore favour, to the fullest possible extent, individual ownership. So that thus far the minister's statement stands just as he made it, and it meets with my approval.
I should like some clarification of the minister's stand with respect to state-created money, and its use. The social credit stand, as I said on that earlier occasion, is that money which it is possible for the state to have created within it, ought to belong to the people of the state, and should be issued by the government as a clear asset to the government, free of debt. It should be administered by the government in the interests of all the people of the state. The other night the minister entirely agreed with that proposition. He and I may not agree as to just what the best disposition of the money would be, but it is good to know that our hearts are in the same place so far as the desire to use money for the welfare of the people is concerned.
The matter of state-created money is of great importance. One must consider how much can be used, and whether the state issue of money will cause inflation. The observations last night of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), addressed to hon. members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, in which he referred to Germany, brought to my attention more vividly the importance of discussing this whole question of inflation. There exists in the world some of the most grotesque distortions imaginable with respect to the whole German story. Men hold opinions so far from the truth as completely to astonish anyone who knows the story of the German inflation in detail. There are similar distortions respecting the assignats of France. The result is that most people are terrified at the mere mention of Germany or of assignats. As a matter of fact there is much for our generation to learn from both those experiments, and what is to be learned from them is entirely in favour of and not against the social credit proposals, strange as that may seem.

As I have said, I should be pleased to take on the Minister of Labour, when he is ready, in a discussion respecting Germany. However it would be better to discuss Germany alone, and not mix it up with this matter, if the minister does not mind.
May I read one more quotation from the same page? The Minister of Finance said:
The reason why the hon. gentleman takes that $26,000,000 is that at that time there was a gold standard, which was departed from to the extent that that $26,000,000 was created. To-day there is no gold standard, and to the extent that we b rrow from the Bank of Canada, as we do to a limited extent, are we not doing exactly what that government did when it issued the $26,000,000?
May I congratulate the minister, after thinking it over, on that statement. It was a brave and progressive thing to say. It acknowledged the truth-truth upon which we can build a good deal of constructive thought.
In the light of that remark I wish to read from Hansard of March 20, 1941, page 1724 the answer given by the minister to a question asked by the hon. member for Acadia. I should like the minister to clarify the situation, bearing in mind what is contained in the following question and answer:
Mr. Quelch: Up to the present time the government have not used the Bank of Canada for the purpose of obtaining money to meet current expenditures, apart from refunding and the purchase of gold? That is really what I wish to know.
Mr. Usley: No.

speechtext:
I realize a question like that is a difficult one for the minister to deal with, because of the tremendous complexity and immensity of the work he has in his mind. But we are vitally concerned as to whether or not the government does issue money from the Bank of Canada and does use that money for ordinary governmental purposes. For example, would the minister consider it sound to issue money from the Bank of Canada to the extent of, say $100,000,000, to buy gold from the refineries, so that the money so issued would go out directly into circulation in Canada? It is obvious that a distinct difference in policy would be involved. In one case the money never leaves the Bank of Canada; it is merely transferred from one drawer or one room to another. In the other case the money would go right out into circulation, as did the $26,000,000 at the time of the last war. That would establish an entirely different policy. I am not going to ask the minister to make a statement on it now, because he will need to look into the matter. But in order that there may be the similarity between the social credit concept and the government concept which the minister's words and my words would tend to indicate, it is necessary that the government be ready to issue money from the Bank of Canada, and buy gold right out in the country, wherever it can be obtained, direct from the mine. There would follow this conclusion, that if the government could issue notes of the Bank of Canada and buy gold in Canada from the refineries, it ought to be equally sound for the government to issue such money and buy wheat. The only difference would be that the gold, in one case, could be put into the vaults of the government or of the bank, and held as a sort of guarantee for the money issued. In the other case there would be wheat in possession of the government.
As the minister recognizes, this is a most important matter, because if the Bank of Canada could issue money to buy wheat, and the government could obtain that money without debt and without taxing the people, then there would be a way open for a possible solu-i tion of many problems troubling us to-day. I have raised this question so that everyone may see the difference between the concept of the social creditors, if there is a difference, and the concept of the government.
Another passage from the minister's remarks, to be found on page 3111 of Hansard, is as follows:
We are not going into debt when we borrow from the Bank of Canada because we are the Bank of Canada.
War Appropriation

With that I entirely agree.
Therefore, the difference between the hon. gentleman and myself comes down to this, does it not, merely a matter of judgment as to how far we should go in borrowing from the Bank of Canada?
Mr. Blackmore: I think so.
I had to be careful about what words I used, because I lacked the knowledge which the minister could give me as a result of the questions I have asked to-day. The question as to how far we should go being merely a matter of judgment is a sound question; I Should like to comment briefly on it before going on to other aspects of the whole question.
As I said the other day, the idea has got abroad-by the way, I have a statement from a bank manager contained in a bank letter this year which conveys the idea that if the government were to create a dollar bill, that dollar bill would be inflation. That is an utter fallacy; it is one of the most dangerous concepts that could be foisted upon mankind at the present stage of our affairs. The issue of new money would not be inflation. Inflation is the rise of prices only. Until the new money, even if it were hundreds of millions, began to cause a rise in prices, it would not be inflation. If the members of this house could agree to that truth, a great amount of the anxiety which now prevails in this country from shore to shore, and a great many of the anxieties of the government, would be allayed. I laid down this principle the other day and I wish to lay it down to-day: The amount of money which can be issued by the government and used depends upon the goods-and-services-producing-and-consuming-power of the country.
May I revert briefly to the German situation. The reason why Germany came into financial disaster was largely this:	that
Germany as a country was relatively poor and small, while her population was relatively large. The goods-and-services-producing-and-consuming-power of Germany did not justify the creation of as much money as was created in Germany. I shall discuss this at greater length when the Minister of Labour and I have our little friendly discussion.
It is not entirely a matter of judgment; at least in forming judgment one is not entirely without realities to go by. One knows that the amount of money which could be issued in Canada depends, for example, on the amount of milk that Canada can produce and consume, on the amount of butter, the amount of lumber, the amount of sugar, the amount of honey, the amount of vegetables and fruit, the amount of coal and gasoline and all other

things which Canada can produce and consume. Production and consumption are vitally bound up in the whole question of inflation. The minister indicated that he understood this in a speech which he made-a fine speech, upon which I would commend him-on March 17, 1942, to the Ontario federation of agriculture. He indicated quite clearly in that speech that he understood that agriculture and the productive power of agriculture were vital to the monetary situation in Canada; that is, that agriculture had much to do with whether or not Canada was in danger of inflation. That is what I gathered from the minister's speech. May I quote again from page 3112 of Hansard:
Mr. Ilsley: We believe it would be quite unsafe to go any further than we have gone, in view of the danger of inflation. We do not believe we could control inflation by our price ceiling policy if we went much further in the issue of money, because it would burst the price ceiling. If the price ceiling, by some miracle, should hold, then it would mean the indefinite continuance of the price ceiling after the war, because there would be such a volume of bank credit or currency or both that the removal of the price ceiling would be impossible because prices would soar so desperately.
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury):	The whole
theory means inflation; it cannot mean anything else.
By which remark the leader of the opposition indicated that he has a lot more to learn about money. The minister's remarks were quite sound. I should like to draw something to the minister's attention and to the attention of those who are worrying about this problem. After the war there will be a tremendous amount of productive capacity available, productive capacity which is now devoted to the fabrication of war goods. This capacity will be without further employment and will of necessity be diverted immediately or as soon as possible to the production of goods for consumption within the country. If the minister does not have at that time a substantial accumulation of purchasing power in the hands of the people throughout Canada, there will be a serious deficiency of buying power. The result will be that the new production which would be the result of the transfer of the war producing machinery to the production of peace-time goods will not be disposed of and there will be precipitated a most appalling condition of unemployment.
Such a condition would be deflation. I know the minister realizes that there are two serious problems facing any government. The one is to prevent inflation, and the other, equally important, is to prevent deflation. The government must guard against both, and also be prepared to take such measures as are neces-

War Appropriation
sary to ensure the stability of the employment situation after the war. This question is troubling the rank and file of Canadians far more than the danger of inflation. While I recognize that there is a danger of inflation, I believe it could be controlled to a greater extent than it is at the present time, although the government and the minister are doing a commendable work in their efforts to control it.
I wish the leader of the opposition were in the chamber, because I should like to ask him right to his face what he thinks he would do with all the tremendous amount of post-war production if he had an impoverished population. For example, I should like to ask him how he imagines the Canadian people would be able to consume the butter and cheese, particularly the cheese which we are now manufacturing and shipping to Great Britain, and the beef and the pork, unless they had savings. What will happen to the men who are engaged in the production of pork-just as a concrete everyday illustration-if the British market is in some measure closed to us or if we no longer have the tremendous number of sinkings on the seas? What would happen to the men whose money is now or will be invested in pork production? All these are matters of vital concern to the Canadian people, but they are matters which the leader of the opposition has evidently been too busy to consider.
I wish to read one more statement made by the minister. He said, at page 3112 of Hansard:
The hon. gentleman denies that his policy means inflation.
I certainly do; for I say that the social credit proposals are the only means by which inflation can be fully controlled. He goes on:
We argue and believe that it does, if it goes much beyond what we are doing anyway, or probably if it goes at all beyond what we are doing anyway. That is what we believe. We get the best advice we can; we exercise the best judgment we can, and our judgment tells us that we want to withdraw' purchasing power from the consumers of this country. We want desperately to do that, because of the terrific upward pressure on the price level if we do not.
I believe I have been quite fair to the minister. I have tried to select statements he made to show his point of view so that there can be no misunderstanding. I sympathize with the minister in this statement of his. I urge upon the minister that the social credit proposals could be of great assistance to him, as I propose to demonstrate in the course of my remarks.
The first all-important question is, what is inflation? May I give a definition which I believe is absolutely sound? Inflation is a
rise in price which results from having more money in circulation that there are goods in the market to buy with the money; putting it in another way one might say that inflation is a rise of price resulting from a scarcity of goods. In other words, the stress should be placed not only upon money but upon goods. I made the remark to the Minister of Labour last night that the difficulty that Germany faced was that she lacked goods, and the more you examine the story of Germany the more you will realize that that is true. It was fundamentally the shortage of goods in Germany that caused her inflation. We cannot bear in upon our minds too emphatically this fact, that inflation can be controlled by having more goods, more production. That was the great thought which the minister gave in his speech of March 17 to which I have referred.
As an illustration of how state money or any kind of money can be used to prevent inflation, to prevent a rise in price, to increase production, may I elaborate on what the minister is already doing? He is subsidizing prices. Some members of the opposition have been inclined to criticize the minister for spending the amount of money he is spending in subsidizing prices. But in this the minister is wholly sound. He can spend many times the amount of money he is spending on subsidizing and still be doing a work of very great value for the people of Canada. He does not need to be afraid of subsidies, or afraid of his critics; when he said the other day that he would fight an election on that issue he was certainly taking very sound ground. It is possible to spend a large amount of money in a way which according to orthodox principles would seem unsound and yet obtain a result which is of such tremendous value to the state as a whole that the money must appear very well spent.
To illustrate; Great Britain in 1941, I found when I was overseas and talking to a prominent member of the British house, spent 100 million pounds in keeping down the cost of goods to the people. Great Britain in that same year spent 30 million pounds, I was told, in subsidizing the prices of the primary producers. As an illustration, I gathered this from an article I was reading not long ago. The British government are paying the egg producer 75 cents a dozen for eggs and then selling those eggs to the consumer for 50 cents a dozen, which means that on every dozen of eggs the British government is paying out 25 cents; and still that is good business, and for two reasons. In the first place it is a stimulation of the production of a vital necessity, and in the next place it is
War Appropriation

making it possible for the consumer to buy without causing inflation. Some people would say that that kind of procedure, paying 75 cents a dozen for eggs and then selling them for 50 cents, is bound to lead to inflation. Not at all; for on the consumer market, where you judge the impact of inflation, prices have been brought down. If the government had not given 75 cents a dozen for eggs, egg production would have greatly fallen off, and prices would have risen to perhaps SI a dozen. That would mean inflation.
