subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is not profiteering
at all. I think I shall have to stop for just a minute to deal with the hon. member's question. In western Canada to-day the farmers are paying for the 147 things they buy 152 per cent of what they were paying for those same articles in 1914. Now if their costs increase by 52-2 per cent, how in the world can they continue to produce if their prices are not increased? And yet the price of their commodity on the market is lower to-day than it was in 1914. How are you going to bridge that gap? When you get down to reasoning it out, you will be so close to the social credit concept of adjusting the price to the consumer and subsidizing the price to the producer that you will not be able to tell the difference.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
And the taxpayer would
have to pay for it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The taxpayer would
not be paying for it if the money were being created. That is the important principle of state-created money, that prices can be adjusted without taxation or borrowing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I cannot understand
that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There will be those
who cannot understand it, but it can be understood. It is the truth and it is understood by the best thinkers to-day all over the world.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
How would you produce
state money?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
As I said the other
night, you created it during the last war, when the government printed $26,000,000 of new money. They just printed it; they could have created it as credit. The principle in both cases is sound. The printing of that $26,000,000 certainly did not cause inflation. If there was an inflationary tendency it would have been overcome by the application of a price ceiling such as the minister has applied.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, but $26,000,000, comparatively speaking, would not be anything at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The principle is established. I was asked where the money would come from, and I have said where it would come from.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is a pretty easy way to get it, is it not?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is just like anything else; you have to know how and to what extent to do it, and exercise the power with wisdom.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Who knows?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That must be discovered. It depends on the goods-and-services-producing-and-consuming-power of the country. Obviously, if Canada were a desert you could not have any money without having inflation. And the more completely Canada becomes removed from a desert condition the more money she can have. That is obvious.
I wish to go on and finish what I have to say, and after that I shall be delighted to answer questions. I am pleased with the interruption. I have been through these questions a good many times.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But we never know any more.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have known students in classes to go through the subject a dozen times, and yet not know the grammar or the advanced algebra; but there was nothing wrong with the grammar or the advanced algebra.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Perhaps, with the teacher.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Or with the teacher either. I have illustrated the need for subsidies and discounts. I just want to point out to the committee something which is contained in the May 20 issue of the Searle index, to show the conditions now existing in western Canada. I quote:
The present price of wheat is now 43 per cent below the 1913-14 parity price and when the new 90 cent price is established for this new crop it will be 31 per cent below parity. The price of hogs is now 14 per cent below parity and steers 10 per cent below the 1913-14 parity, with lambs 7 per cent above the 1913-14 parity. But the average hourly rates of wages received by industrial labour working at munitions and other war industries is 44 per cent above the 1913-14 parity.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that in that little statement is pictured a set of economic conditions which is threatening and which will ruin this country unless measures are

War Appropriation
adopted to offset it. It challenges every thoughtful man in this country. It is a situation which must be overcome. I turn now to the back page of the same document and read what is stated regarding prices:
The Searle Index of the cost of things farmers buy (147 items) now stands at 152'4 (1913-14 equals 100).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Are those consumer goods?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, they are mainly consumer goods. But they include such capital goods as, we will say, certain kinds of machines. There is a long list of them which I can give the minister. There are such things as post hole diggers, mittens, and other articles farmers buy for use in their ordinary work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: How does the cost of production compare?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Obviously every increase in the cost of articles used by a farmer, is going to increase the cost of producing, let us say, milk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What about his tractors?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They all add to his cost of production.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: And what about the cost of a bushel of wheat?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The costs of producing wheat have all gone up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman sure of that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am sure of it. I can produce a number of figures; in fact the Searle figures are in point. I believe there are hon. members here

the hon. member for Souris and the hon. member for Moose Jaw-who could give them right off. All these costs have gone up astoundingly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. member has spoken for forty minutes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It does not sound over five.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Dealing with the argument as it affects agriculture, and seeing that we have with us the Minister of Labour, I might point out that the other evening I tried to get some information from the Minister of Agriculture, which the Minister of Labour may be able to supply. I believe it is generally realized that prices of agricultural products have been frozen at a very unfair level and have caused us certain difficulties, especially in the harvest months.
These difficulties will be multiplied this fall, and harvest is less than two months away. There are men travelling through the country to-day who do not care to work and who are not much interested in the war effort; they ask rates of pay for harvest work which create great difficulties to the farmers. I believe the man who assists in the harvest field or elsewhere on the farm is entitled to fair remuneration, but I should like to know from the Minister of Labour, under whose jurisdiction this matter comes, whether in his opinion some equitable basis of pay could be worked out and set in operation before harvest time which will be fair both to the farmer and to the labourer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I believe my hon. friend knows, perhaps better than I do, that no attempt has ever been made in this country to regulate harvest wages.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No attempt was ever made before to set price ceilings for produce such as have now been put into effect.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Just a minute; listen to me. I should be very glad if my hon. friend could make any suggestions along this line. If he can, he is just the man I am looking for, and he can rest assured that my office is open to him every day in the week, twenty-four hours a day.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think first of all I should congratulate the Minister of Finance on the success with which he has imbibed the social credit philosophy. We here are beginning to wonder whether the government will be moving over to this side or whether the social credit section of the house will be moving across to the government benches.
There are two or three questions I wanted to bring before the minister in connection with this bill. When it was under discussion before I raised a question with regard to the closing down of the Canadian Associated Aircraft plant. At that time 40 per cent of the employees had already been discharged, and the remainder had received notice that they would be discharged in two weeks' time. The Minister of Munitions and Supply said at that time that these men would be absorbed by the adjoining plant, the National Steel Car company. Word has come that National Steel Car management, in correspondence with the management of Canadian Associated Aircraft, indicates that there is no place whatever in their plant for the personnel of Canadian Associated Aircraft. Can the Minister of Labour tell us whether any provision is made under which these
War Appropriation

aircraft workers, some of them partly and some of them expertly trained, can procure other employment within a few days' time when that plant closes down? I understand that National Steel Car is only in the stage of tuning up for the new bomber which it will produce later.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My department is
already in touch with the situation, and if the men have the skill that my hon. friend says they have, I do not think there should be any great difficulty in their being placed through the employment service.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The second question I wished to raise is this. I have received representations from a number of de Havilland workers who were discharged the latter part of last week. As the minister probably knows, in each case the discharged workers were trade unionists, all taking a prominent part in organizing their trade union in that plant in competition with the company union that the company was fostering. Is there nothing the minister or his department can do to facilitate cooperation between trade union organizations and management within these plants? I have noticed again and again in the plants of which I have some knowledge that just as soon as a group of trade unionists begin to organize a union in a plant, the management immediately sets to work organizing a company union to offset the influence of the trade union, with the result that there is conflict between the employers and employees and production is interrupted. Are there no steps the government can take to prevent that conflict, which arises in nearly every industrial plant in this country? It seems to me it is a matter in respect to which something could be done.
We have heard a great deal of the importance and necessity of oil; and I am sorry the Minister of Munitions and Supply is not here. I believe the government have announced during this session that they are not interested in financing the production of oil in any field- I think that is their policy-but they are willing to promote the production of oil in any field in any way short of actual financing of it. If I am wrong in that I should like to be corrected. I have figures showing that the oil production in the Turner Valley field last year was almost 10,000,000 barrels. Forty-one new wells were brought into production. Of that number twenty-five were private or independent wells financed by the sale of royalties. I am informed that 40 per cent of the present production in that field is produced by these independently financed wells. The sixteen new wells brought into production by the oil companies which control large areas

there are all, I am told, offsetting wells brought into production only to prevent the independent companies from drawing the oil from their properties. They all adjoin wells which had already been brought into production by independent companies.
It seems to me that the government should facilitate in every possible way the development of oil wells. I am told that there are only two methods by which the opening of these wells can be financed : one by the sale of royalties to the public, and the other by the big oil companies. Apparently at the present time it is not the policy of the big oil companies to bring their wells into production. My information is-and again if the minister has more recent or more accurate information we should have it-that the big oil companies have more than a hundred proven wells in that valley that are capped at the present time and not producing, and that they are producing only where it is necessary to offset some well brought into production by the independent producers.
It has been called to my attention that the salesmen interested in the financing of these independent wells, twenty-five of which were brought into production last year, are prevented from carrying on further work by reason of the fact that the oil controller allows them only an A category gasoline ration. I have a report here of the negotiations carried on with the oil controller, showing that he changed his mind at least a half a dozen times on this subject. At first he granted these salesmen a higher category; then the books were called in, or some of them, and some were left with category A, others with category E, and final decision was reached that no one interested in the sale of oil royalities should have anything more than A category. In view of the fact that by that means twenty-five wells were brought into production in 1941 it seems reasonable that the government should encourage further opening of wells by that means.
Another matter that I should like to call to the minister's attention is a suggestion concerning our rubber supply, particularly salvage rubber. A number of dealers interested in preserving our rubber supply have made to me the following representations, which I pass on to the proper authorities.
My attention has been called to the fact that there are thousands of tons of salvage rubber at the present time left exposed to sun and weather. No attempt has been made by the government to see that these thousands of tons are protected in any way from the elements. There is no regulation under which

War Appropriation
the usable part of that salvage rubber, consisting of tires many of which can be vulcanized and used, is separated from the scrap. My information is that at present large quantities of tires which could be vulcanized and used again are in the junk piles and no effort is being made to separate them. So far as I can discover, there is nothing in the regulations to prevent second-hand dealers from hoarding all the second-hand tires they can acquire. It is true the government has a record of these, but I am informed that there are second-hand rubber dealers who are hoarding large quantities of this material. On the same subject of leaving tires exposed, if you look at the second-hand car lots of this country you will find thousands of tons of tires exposed to the weather, deteriorating, on cars which, in view of the gasoline situation, probably will not be used for years. I seriously believe that if rubber is so scarce, some steps should be taken to save these thousands of tires from deterioration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think the first question asked by the hon. member was with regard to discrimination at the de Havilland plant at Montreal, was it not?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No; at Toronto.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Very well. I do not know whether my hon. friend is aware of the fact, but order in council P.C. 4020 gives the Minister of Labour power to send in a commissioner and to act upon the recommendations of that commissioner, and the action of the minister is final and binding on both parties. I would say to my hon. friend that almost from day to day we hear of cases of alleged discrimination on both sides. At the moment we have five permanent commissioners, one located in the west, one in the middle west, one in Ontario, one in Montreal, and one for the maritimes. I remember quite vividly that when I was chairman of the industrial disputes inquiry commission we dealt with a number of cases of the nature of the one to which my hon. friend referred, and in every case we were able to arrange a satisfactory settlement. I am sure my hon. friend appreciates that in the process of organization tempers sometimes become frayed on both sides, and that order in council has been of great service not only to the employees but also to the employers. If my hon. friend cares to look up that order in council, he will find the provision to which I have referred in section 5.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
This afternoon the hon.
member for Rosetown-Biggar brought up the question of the Dumart plant and asked the Minister of Labour if it was the intention of
the government to place a controller in that plant in accordance with the wishes of the employees. The minister categorically replied that it was not. That plant has been closed for some four weeks. It is an essential industry. Bacon is practically under government control; the bacon board demands a certain quota from each plant each month, and there is no doubt that the attitude of the operator of that plant is interfering with the war effort.
This dispute had its origin in a trivial matter; two employees were dismissed over a slight argument, and as a result there was a walk-out of the employees. The same evening a representative of the Department of Labour arrived on the scene, and, after negotiation, felt he had the matter settled. He went to bed that night in the belief that the dispute had been satisfactorily settled, as far as the workers were concerned and, as he thought, also to the satisfaction of the employer. The employees reported for work at seven o'clock the following morning, and were notified that the plant was not open; evidently the employer changed his mind overnight. The situation at present is that this is an illegal lock-out. That is not my version of it; the representative of the Department of Labour, who was sent to negotiate the dispute, made that declaration publicly. For some four weeks the employers have refused to open that plant. The union which functions there is of the government's own brand; it is an employees' committee, and the employees are under contract with the plant. One of the provisions of the contract is that ail disputes must be taken up with the local superintendent. The man who dismissed the two employees was not the local but the general superintendent, which placed the local superintendent in a position where he could not very well settle the matter in accordance with the terms of the contract without going over the head of his superior. The situation is in quite a tangle now, and I think it is time someone took hold of it and tried to do something about it. Some three weeks ago I had the privilege of meeting a committee from that plant, just a couple of boys and a couple of girls who had not very much of an idea what it was all about, who came here to see me.
I am not going to elaborate the matter further. I say it is absolute neglect on the part of someone. I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Labour, however, to an editorial appearing in this afternoon's Ottawa Journal, dealing with a speech delivered by the director of national selective service to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. It is well worth reading by anyone interested in relations between employer
War Appropriation

and employee. He makes an observation which I think is pertinent, having in mind the attitude of the management at the Dumart plant:
To those who don't want good relations or don't appreciate their value, I say: The country cannot afford to have you as an employer at any time, particularly in war time. You must change your ways. . . .
Waving a flag in a workman's face and calling on his patriotism cannot be a substitute for decent treatment. You cannot write a memo about it, and accomplish it. . . . It must be an attitude, a frame of mind, a recognition of existing facts and conditions which can be turned to mutual advantage for an employer and employee-and for the country.
I believe that statement is absolutely pertinent to this case. The employer is wrong. He is interfering with an essential industry. The matter was settled by arbitration. There is nothing in the dispute to-day that should keep this plant idle, except stubbornness on the part of the employer. The employees want to return to work one hundred per cent, including the two men who were dismissed, and then they are willing to have the matter arbitrated. They are prepared to go before any board of arbitration and negotiate what may be in the mind of the employer or any grievances they may have. Their contract has been violated. The general superintendent, in precipitating this trouble, placed the management, the local superintendent and the employees in a position where they are deadlocked, and the plant is closed. I think it is time the Minister of Labour or someone demonstrated the attitude of mind which Mr. Little mentioned in the remarks I quoted.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Will they go back to
work without the two men who were dismissed?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is no reason why
they should. The plant has been idle for a month now. The dispute was over nothing in the first place; it had to do with a short period they had at the noon hour. The two men dismissed were working at the far end of the line, and when the dinner hour arrived, as I understand it, they got away five or ten minutes later than the other employees, but they came back at the same time. As a result they were not getting sufficient time to complete their meal, and they merely requested that they be allowed the extra time they had to stay on the line after the other workers left. For that they were dismissed. I just happened to come across a parallel case which occurred in Britain, and perhaps it is worth while putting it on record. This concerned the dismissal of a woman in a plant. The union presented their case; the 
management presented their case, exactly as was done in the present instance. The matter went to a court, which found that while the employees did not do right in walking out, nevertheless it was the only way they had to demonstrate in order to assist the woman who was dismissed for a reason which was found insufficient to tie up a plant. The matter was straightened out in that way. The court of arbitration in Great Britain decided in that manner, and for four weeks the employers in the plant have sat back and refused either to recognize common sense or loss, or the seriousness of the war situation, or the essentiality of their plant in that setting.
On the basis of the Kirkland Lake dispute, and many other disputes which have taken place across Canada I say it is high time somebody got down to business, and set up a court with a man like Elliott M. Little at the head of it. My opinion is that it is a disgrace to have a plant of that kind tied up for four weeks-and to all intents and purposes the same situation is going to continue. I myself cannot understand what the trouble is. Through one of its officials the Department of Labour have declared this an illegal lockout. If to-morrow there is an illegal strike, what happens? The Minister of Labour immediately places the responsibility on the Department of Justice, and those responsible for fomenting and carrying on the illegal strike are tried and interned. For example, C. S. Jackson was interned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not for an illegal strike, was he?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Jackson was interned for that strike in Toronto at the General Electric plant.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: And for lesser allegations than that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would not argue the point, but that is the way I feel about the matter. If one of the minister's officials publicly states that this is an illegal lock-out, and it is carried on for four weeks, is it not about time that it was passed on to somebody else for some action? Certainly that plant should be working.
I have no intention of labouring the matter further. I spoke this afternoon because the matter had been discussed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I had the privilege of sitting in on the committee. I saw a couple of boys and girls who are willing to work, but who are certainly not in a position themselves, with their knowledge of affairs, to arbitrate and to get a fair settlement in the matter.

War Appropriation
If the Minister of Labour and his department, who are experienced in these matters, are not prepared to take hold and see that matters are settled to the satisfaction of all concerned, then something else will have to be done. The trouble can spread.
The Bums packing plant is a big organization. Packing plant workers in Canada belong to a powerful trade union, and they have powerful international affiliations. I do not think they are going to sit back much longer and allow a certain portion of their workers to starve in the street, in the present circumstances, without some justification. The natural procedure is to support those people.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
As my hon. friend is well aware, I have never taken the position, and do not now intend to do so, that it is in the public interest immediately to take over a plant because a group of workers or employers act in opposition to government policy. I should like that to be clearly understood.
I am not going to discuss with my hon. friend whether this was a lock-out or an illegal strike. As he knows, since I have been Minister of Labour I have decentralized the conciliation service of the dominion and placed it under the jurisdiction of provincial governments. That was done primarily because there had been some delay in facing up to industrial disputes. The settlement of the dispute in question was under the jurisdiction of a provincial department of labour. I believe that is a fact which may readily be agreed upon. May I add that there has been considerable trouble at Dumarts, ever since the place was organized. I believe that can be freely admitted. There was ample provision under some of the orders in council which have received criticism from certain people in the dominion to take care of the situation which arose there. The people at Dumarts knew it. Let us keep the record straight on that point.
It should be stated that the strike took place when the business agent was having a discussion with the management. The management claimed that the language used by the two people discharged was not the kind of language which should be used. Possibly it was the language of the slaughterhouse- because we know that miners, electricians and engineers do not always use the most pleasant language at times.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Very expressive, though.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Hon. members will see
the difficult position in which it places a minister of labour, whether he be a minister in the Ontario government, or myself. When people go on an illegal strike a minister's hands are immediately tied.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
But it lasted only about
four hours.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is not important.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Your official settled it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There must be discipline in these matters; let us be fair. As I said this afternoon, when I was chairman of the industrial disputes inquiry commission I looked into disputes of this kind on many occasions. I could have sent a commissioner in within twenty-four hours, and got back his report, as we have done on many occasions. But the company claimed that these people left their employ, rightly or wrongly, and they contend that a good deal of business had been lost through this dispute.
I have always felt that there was a grave risk in putting people out on the street. My hon. friend will agree with me that that is one of the easiest things in the world.-to have men and women on the street. But sometimes it is not so easy to get them back to work. Industrial leadership is the fly-wheel. There must be leadership on both sides; sometimes it breaks one way, and sometimes the other way. But if we took that leadership away, whether it be among the employers or the employees, I am afraid industrial conditions in this country would be in a very grave state.
I suppose for many years I have been as close to the rank and file as most people in the labour movement of Canada. I have found on every occasion that if people are given the right kind of leadership, one can take them out or leave them in-as long as one is frank with them. For instance, in my own trade, in my own city, we were among the highest paid in the dominion. Yet we never had a strike, during the whole of our existence. That is why we were among the highest paid in the dominion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But you had good wages and good conditions; there was no necessity to call the men out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not always.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
These things were not all
handed to you on a platter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I appreciate that.
May I say with regard to Kirkland Lake that I am quite prepared to discuss the whole matter at another time. As I said, however, at the moment the Dumart dispute is in the hands of a provincial government-and I am not saying that to get out from under any responsibility in the matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Where does the angle of war production come in? Do you turn over
War Appropriation

all these disputes to provincial governments, or are matters affecting materials essential to the war not handled from the dominion department?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The plant is not closed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yesterday I asked the minister a question as reported on page 3126 of Hansard. The question was:
Is the order recently made by the national war labour board of Canada fixing the wages of common labour in the Yukon at 75 cents per hour plus cost of living bonus being enforced against all employers of common labour in Yukon?
The minister's answer was an unequivocal yes, but he went on to give certain facts which showed that his answer was a conditional yes. The fact is that the order is being enforced against Canadian employers and Canadian employees and not against foreign employers and foreign employees working in that part of Canada. The minister explained the necessity of hastening the construction of the Alaska highway for the defence of Canada and the United States. I say to him and to this committee that if the immediate defence of the United States and Alaska and Canada are dependent upon the completion of the Alaska highway, it is too late. At the present moment great numbers of fighting men and large quantities of mechanical equipment and weapons can be moved from the United States and Canada into Alaska without the use of the Alaska highway. These goods and men can be taken in by boat and by rail, and there is no limit upon what can be carried. I contend that to enforce the order of the Canadian wartime labour board as to wages for work in Yukon, wages paid by all employers and earned by all employees, would not hinder or delay the construction of that highway, the use of which is not immediately necessary because other and better means of transportation are available. I say that it is manifestly unfair to the Canadian wage-earners to limit the Canadian wartime labour board's order to the wages paid to them. I maintain that that order should be applied to all employers and employees in Yukon, Canada, regardless of nationality. It is not correct to say that the foreigner must pay and receive higher wages than the Canadian in order to hasten the completion of that highway. If the minister were a Canadian labourer working on that highway job, I am sure that he would not approve his own policy or the policy of his government. I ask him and I ask the government to

War Appropriation
enforce that wartime labour board's order without favouritism and without exception. It is the only fair and proper thing to do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
First of all, I am not going into matters of high strategy with my hon. friend. I am not going to discuss whether troops should be moved to Alaska or to the Yukon by ship or by rail. I am one of those who think that this war is going to last another ten years, although I hope I am wrong. We may be very glad to have that road before the war is over. The other day my hon. friend drew to my attention the fact that wage rates in northern British Columbia were getting out of control. Agents of United States contractors were going through the west recruiting labour for the Alaska highway. We acted with about as much expedition as we could and arranged a conference through external affairs with United States government representatives in an effort to overcome some of the disagreeable conditions that some think exist to-day in Newfoundland.
My hon. friend knows as well as I about the tremendous shortage of labour that will follow the building of this Alaska highway up through British Columbia and Alberta and also the highway from Prince Rupert to a point to the east. It will be necessary to recruit thousands of men, many of them skilled men, in the United States. In order to do that, it will be necessary to pay the going rates in the different communities in the United States where the men may be recruited. It is a general practice of law that when United States citizens work abroad they shall be paid a bonus of 25 per cent for foreign service. Then there is the matter of the exchange on the United States dollar. I do not need to tell my hon. friend what bearing this will have upon wages and prices in British Columbia when these men come to work during the ensuing summer months.
It was agreed between the representatives of the governments that the Canadian contractors should employ Canadians and that the United States contractors would have the right to bring in labour from the other side. As far as the Canadians were concerned the workmen's compensation and the unemployment insurance benefits would prevail. United States conditions would prevail for the United States workmen. It was suggested also that the United States workmen should be advised to remit as much of their wages to the United States as they possibly could. I do not know of a more practicable way of dealing with the matter.
I appreciate that to some the rates of wages for unskilled labour in that part of the country
may seem high, but I know something about board costs there. I think we all know something about the climatic conditions that prevail, the mosquitoes and the black flies. I think my hon. friend will agree that this thing should be given a trial in order that we may try to overcome some of the difficulties that may exist at the moment in Newfoundland. Our wage policy in northern British Columbia and Alberta must be such as to meet the tremendous demands for labour to build the Alaska highway.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I can only repeat that I think Canadian laws should prevail, that the foreigner should be subject to them just as must as we are.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is a lovely theory, but it does not always work, and I do not say that in any critical way. In connection with unemployment insurance and social security measures, there is already an arrangement between the United States government and our own which permits certain persons, particularly those who work on the railroads, to retain pension rights, social security rights, workmen's compensation rights and so on in the United States. The same condition prevails with respect to certain Canadians. From my point of view that is all to the good. If this exchange of opinions and services that has existed as between the dominion and the United States had existed in Europe, I do not think we would be fighting this war to-day. I cannot imagine, for instance, the French government owning a railroad to Berlin in the same way as the Canadian government owns that prosperous piece of track running from Port Huron to Chicago. In all these matters we find there is a necessity for the interchange of regulations and prohibitions between the two countries. Do not forget that the United States is paying for the Alaska highway, and we are not.

speechtext: True, the United States is paying for it, and Canada is letting the United States build it through Canada, but I say again that it is not fair to the Canadian workmen to make them work for 75 cents an hour, while an American working alongside him and doing the same work gets $1.05 an hour.

speechtext: But the understanding is that United States contractors will employ United States labour and they will be in their own camps. Canadians and Americans will not be working alongside one another as is generally understood of work on a construction gang, but there will be United States camps and Canadian camps, miles apart. If the Americans are going to recruit shovel runners, truck operators, what they call operating engineers in construction engineering-and I understand they will need about three thousand of them-I imagine that it will be necessary to get them from the places where these men can- be found in the United States. I think I know something of the wage structure in that industry, and the only way you can get those men to go to Alaska is to pay them the proper rate, just as Canadian contractors will pay the prevailing rates for that part of the country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not get a chance to ask the minister about farm labour. He said that no government had ever attempted to handle that problem before.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I said no Canadian
government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
And no Canadian government has ever handled the price ceiling before. The minister asked what I would suggest. I would remind him that last fall, on November 10, I appealed to the government to introduce national selective service at that time for industry, agriculture and the armed forces, and I pointed out that there were many good men in industry and agriculture who were worth ever so much more there than they could be in the armed forces. I know a young foreman in my own neighbourhood who was operating a very large farm. He did not want to go into the armed forces, but on the other hand he did not want people to say that he had not offered his services. He could render many times the service to this nation in managing that farm that he could in the armed forces; nevertheless he joined up.
The Prime Minister of this country delivered his man-power speech on March 24 of this year, but notwithstanding that speech nothing has been done to this day with respect to applying national selective service to agriculture. Great inequities prevail. Organized labour has been guaranteed a fixed price for its labour, using 1926-29 as the base period. Later on it was guaranteed a cost of living bonus, and there was a guarantee of salaries in industry. I think it would only be just if the government set

a ceiling price for agricultural products, taking the same base period, and guaranteed the farm labourers the same rate of pay, plus a cost of living bonus. Farming is essential in carrying on the war, and I cannot see why the government should not guarantee a rate of wages to both farm labour and organized labour on exactly the same basis. There is a great disparity in the price ceiling, for instance, on butter fat, with a price of 50 cents a pound when it is used in making cheese and 35 cents a pound when it is used in making butter-a product that comes from the very same cow. There are many inequities to-day, and I think it would be reasonable to guarantee a ceding price for agricultural products and to guarantee wages for the farm labourer, all on the same base period.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend mentions selective service. If I remember correctly, the first thing which the department did after the Prime Minister's speech was to freeze labour on the farms. That was the first industry we attacked.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In what respect?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No man working on the farm could leave it and go into industry without a permit. With respect to farm labour this summer, I might say that last year we had an agreement with Ontario, which felt there was going to be a shortage of labour in agriculture; the dominion government matched dollar ^or dollar with the province, up to an expenditure of $60,000 by the dominion, to provide farm labour, and under this scheme 23,000 persons were recruited for farms in Ontario. I think it is agreed that while there may have been difficulties, there was no acute shortage of labour in Ontario to harvest the crops. I discussed the very question my hon. friend now raises with the Minister of Agriculture last February, and we immediately set in motion a policy somewhat similar to that which we adopted with respect to Ontario last year. This year we are prepared to match dollar for dollar with Ontario up to an amount of $100,000, and we are hopeful that with the same enthusiasm and ingenuity the farm labour problem will be solved in Ontario again this year. I have enough faith in the vim and vigour of the Ontario government, working in cooperation with our own, to believe that we shall be able to meet the farm labour problem in Ontario satisfactorily this summer. Similar offers have been made to all the other provincial governments, but apparently they wish to handle the matter themselves, and after all, that is sound policy, for the best kind of government in some things is the one which is closest to the people.

War Appropriation
Up to date we have had no request for similar assistance to that which we are giving to Ontario.
My hon. friend speaks of a cost of living bonus for farm labourers. It has been my good fortune or otherwise to be concerned with a good deal of labour and social legislation in this country, both federal and provincial, and unfortunately much of it exempts agriculture just as it exempts fishing and, to some degree, logging. In certain countries of the British commonwealth, in Britain, in New Zealand, and to a lesser degree in Australia, established rates have been set for farm workers. In this country our problem is a seasonal one created by conditions over which we have no control. I am a comparatively young man, but I hope to live to see the day when we shall set up in this dominion for the employment of men and women on the farm a scheme similar to that prevailing to-day in New Zealand or Britain or Australia. So far as the farm labour problem this year is concerned, I am hopeful that with the assistance of the Employment Service of Canada and the cooperation of the provincial governments, and, more important still, the cooperation of the people most vitally affected, the farmers, themselves, we shall be able to face up to the labour problem in every province during the coming year, notwithstanding the apparent shortage of labour particularly for war industries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Just to follow up the minister's answer about freezing labour on the farms: I do not think that is definite enough. I would remind him of the example I gave of the young man, thirty-five years of age, who is an efficient tractor mechanic, and who has the faculty of handling men. I suggest we ought to be in a position to tell that man where he can give the best service. He does not want to be in a position where, in spite of his efficiency, he will have to meet his pals who have come back from overseas, while he has stayed at home in a machine shop or on a farm. That sort of thing would be avoided if we had a national selective service system under which the government would have authority to say to that chap, "You will be rendering a greater service by remaining where you are; that is where you belong." He would be more than pleased. We have been too haphazard about the whole matter. We cannot get action with regard to it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I may tell my hon. friend, with regard to what he has mentioned, that is the purpose of the whole order, and this question is receiving consideration at this
very moment, because, next perhaps to price regulation and wage stabilization, it is the biggest job which has been tackled during the war. He can rest assured that we are working, with all the speed that health and strength will permit, to launch a policy which we think will receive the approval of the Canadian people in the not too distant future.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
This is a unique opportunity for members of parliament to discuss each of the departments, whether military or civilian. There is a main difference between the legislation that is before the committee and the estimates, in this sense, that when the estimates are brought up each minister must come in turn to answer the questions of the members, but in this case all ministers should be present to answer any questions from any hon. member on any item in their departments. Therefore, sir, it is my privilege and pleasure to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon his assiduity, and also his colleagues who have been here to answer questions from members, and I pay due compliment to the Minister of Labour, who has done fairly well in spite of the difficulties of the present time. I extend the same compliments and pay the same tributes to his colleagues who are here. But I shall have just a few questions to submit.
In the first place I would remind the members of the cabinet of a question which was asked of me at the meeting of the federation of mayors and municipalities here in Ottawa a couple of years ago, when the mayor of a city in beautiful Prince Edward Island, after I had been speaking of the work of the works progress administration in the United States, said, "Do you mean that we should imitate everything that is done in the United States?" My answer was, "No; we should imitate only what we think is the very best, because when we imitate everything it is not imitation; it is just aping." In that connection what strikes me is the reference to what is done in other countries, and the suggestion, which follows, that a thing is good provided we can say that it is done in any other dominion, in the United States, or in any other friendly country. This afternoon one of our colleagues went further and quoted to us the example of Germany with regard to monetary matters. Of course, we shall always benefit from the experience and wisdom of others. On the other hand, however, judicious selection should be made between what suits and what cannot suit this country. Therefore, sir, what I deeply regret is a complete lack of
War Appropriation

imagination, in the adoption of everything that is done outside Canada and that is known to us.
The second thing I have to bring before this committee is the apt remark which was made by the Minister of National Defence- some time in May, if I am not mistaken- when he said that one of the troubles of his department was that his officials could hardly make a distinction between what was essential and what was non-essential. It is very easy for any man or woman working in the office of a cabinet minister to deceive him, if that man or woman is unworthy, by putting on top of the files letters of no consequence at all and matters which unduly distract the minister's attention, and thus prevent him from reaching the essential and crucial points which he has to decide for the solution of any important problem.
I am in full sympathy with the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Labour and their colleagues, and, with all my colleagues of the house who are now sitting in committee I pledge my support to them inasmuch and just as generously as I can give it. But they should not be under the false impression that criticism is hostile. Criticism may be hostile, but no one has the right to forget that most of the time criticism is constructive, and criticism from members of parliament is the more constructive because they have the opportunity of seeing things which ministers will never see, on account of the fact that the treatment given to ministers and to members of parliament by this dominion bureaucracy is altogether different, and that when a minister tells his secretary, "Telephone Mr. So-and-so for such a thing," the answer is always, "yes"; but when a member of parliament does the same thing, the answer is, most of the time, "We regret very much that it is impossible to do what you ask."
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
This bill introduces a new set-up in legislation. As has been pointed out, it is altogether different from the customary practice. It would be interesting to know what could be suggested to be done by all departments other than the war departments to cooperate with the war departments so that we might have the most complete war effort in this country. What struck me was to read not long ago that in the United

States the war effort so far as the steel industry was concerned was not considered complete although it was said to be 98 per cent. In this country the same question could be put with regard to each phase of our war effort. In the first place, in my humble view, the first country to consider is our own. We should never forget the particular interest of Canada in dealing with any other country. Patriotism is more than an ordinaiy quality; it is the virtue par excellence of citizenship; it is love of the land on which one is born or which one has adopted as his own country.
After the last war there was the treaty of Versailles and the establishment of the League of Nations at Geneva, which seemed to broaden the scope of patriotism but, in fact, deformed it. It is very sad to think that a good Canadian by birth or by heart is not given as much consideration in this country as a migratory bird who comes here only for the duration, and who is considered ipso jacto as an expert, endowed with all knowledge and exempt from all criticism.
What I want in each branch of each department of this government is a real Canadian spirit which will serve as an inspiration and guide to all those who have to give their utmost cooperation to the head of the department, who is the minister. It seems that after the complete failure of the League of Nations, a failure that was acknowledged by two prime ministers of Britain, Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Baldwin, before the beginning of this war, we should put utopias aside and come back to the old tradition which has been the strength of this country in years past.
I will take the list of the various departments that we read in this bill. I put in the first place the Department of Justice, because it is the department that interests us, the lawmakers of this country, most. Our statute book has been revised time and time again. We have been told that there are too many legislative bodies in Canada. There was too much legislation in this country even before this war began. We need think only of the statute books coming out yearly from our legislative bodies, from this parliament and the legislatures of the nine provinces. Who is the lawyer, however eminent he may be, who has made himself familiar with each one of those pieces of legislation?
Now, since the start of this war, conditions have completely changed, and it is impossible for us lawmakers, not only to be familiar with, but to follow the legislation by order in council, which is tremendously large and which comes, I would say, by the dozen. I will not

ll'ar Appropriation
ask my colleagues if they are familiar with the statutes of all the provinces. I would ask them if they know anything of the 24,000 orders in council which I am told have been passed since the beginning of this war. I would draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that a distinction should be made between orders in council of a strictly legislative nature and those of an administrative nature, so that members of parliament may be informed, and in turn may inform their electors, as to the so-called progress of legislation by order in council. As was suggested the other day, it would be helpful to have a sort of loose-leaf system, so that very little time would be required to find what was needed. In reply to that suggestion we may be told that these orders in council are published in book form; that five of these books already have been issued, and that we are to have another in the near future. Here again, however, my complaint is that these books containing orders in council are not complete. We have evidence of that fact in the statement made by the Prime Minister the other day in reply to the hon. member for Lake Centre, when the Prime Minister said that it was most difficult to give a complete enumeration of the orders in council of a legislative nature; and, if my memory serves me aright, he added that such a distinction was not made in the office of the privy council, and suggested that my hon. friend get in touch with the clerk of the privy council and discuss the matter with him.
Sometimes members of parliament are told that their questions are long, or that it would be expensive to answer them. But many times members of parliament have asked for facts or information supposed to be before the minister, if the minister was familiar with his department. Many times during sittings of committees I noticed that people did not know how to w'ork. They had to be told how to do their work; they did not know at which end to start. They had to be told what to do, step by step, and then when it was all done they were proud of themselves. But mark you, sir, many questions which are termed extravagant should not be called such without knowing their background, and very often a question asked by a private member is of great assistance to the minister who secures the information from his officials. So my suggestion in regard to the Department of Justice, with all due deference to the minister, is to ask him kindly to come to the help of members of parliament by making information as to legislation easier of access and more available to them, and therefore more available to the people of Canada.
The second department in importance is naturally the Department of Finance. This year we legislate almost entirely in regard to finance, and therefore we must be interested in the financial structure of this country. I remember the electoral propaganda of the province of Ontario at the time when it had leaders like Blake, Cartwright, Mills, Alexander Mackenzie, Mowat and many others who were fighting for provincial rights, as Mercier in the province of Quebec was fighting for equal rights. I remember the discussions carried on by Sir Lomer Gouin and the then Conservative premier of Ontario in regard to increased provincial subsidies, discussions that remind us of those which took place not long ago. We want a sound financial structure for this dominion. At times the minister must find it hard to say no when a request is made of him, and I am sure he is greatly pleased when it is possible for him to say yes. But he will never be mistaken if he takes with a grain of salt all extravagant suggestions that are made outside of the regular lines of logic, because there must be logic in finance as in any other science. While large sums are required at the present time for the prosecution of this war, the minister will realize that in the long run the dominion government will benefit by respecting provincial autonomy. At present there are officials in the employ of the treasury of each province who have shown themselves to be men of experience, who know their business. It would be most unfortunate if they should be ignored or put aside, so that they would not exercise the same responsibilities they have discharged for so many years, during which time they gained experience not only in the collection of taxes but also in the distribution of public money.
My further suggestion to the Minister of Finance is to give an opportunity to members of parliament to submit their views to him, not only with regard to taxation but with regard to the general policy of his department. After having heard all they have to say he would be in a better position to make decisions. I am not complaining about the minister. He is most accessible, and I know he is open-minded. But I should like him to give members of parliament an opportunity to discuss his policies before they are enacted, rather than after they are enforced.
The third civilian department in importance is, naturally, the Department of Labour. There are two things with which that department is not familiar enough. One of them is the fact that there is still unemployment in Canada. Those who deal with the subject are satisfied with what they read in the
War Appropriation

papers, and are under the impression that there is not a man in this country who is willing to work who does not have that opportunity.
I congratulate the hon. member for Cape Breton South upon what he said yesterday and to-day. His manner of speaking reminded me of an able debater whose memory still survives in this chamber; I refer to the Hon. H. H. Stevens. I do not want the Minister of Labour to think that because the hon. member for Cape Breton South made some apt suggestions he was at all antagonistic. I am sure he was not. But he did want to bring the case of miners in his constituency to the attention of the minister, and in doing so he served them very well.
The minister knows that a man whose condition of health is good, but who has passed the military age, cannot get into the army. He knows, too, that there are many young men who have been declared physically unfit, and who cannot secure work. It seems to me that the Department of Labour should have a thorough investigation made by the officers in the unemployment insurance branch, and that the facts gathered thereby should be submitted by the Minister of Labour to the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Public Works so that it may be seen what can be done to relieve unemployment and to contribute in a high degree toward increasing the war effort by distributing useful work among those at present unemployed.
Is it not possible to improve our highways, our links of communication between the various provinces, between Canada and the Yukon on the Pacific side or between the St. Lawrence river basin and the United States on the eastern side. This is a policy I have advocated for a long time. I have pointed out that our means of communication should be improved, and the men who are now unemployed are precisely those who could do that work. It would be a most useful work, one which would be necessary and, in fact, indispensable in the event of attack from an enemy. This is what should be done: How long and how often must we repeat it to have it understood? This is not a matter of patronage; it is a matter of protecting the country against any invader, and it is essential to our very lives. These things could be done easily, and without disturbing the war effort or the technicians, because it is done by manual labour.
I warmly congratulate my dear friend the former speaker, the hon. member for Yukon, upon the stand he took this afternoon when he 
refreshed the memory of the government about the road to the Yukon. What has been done about this road? We have heard about it for a long time. For some time we were told that we were not to build a highway, but that a railway was to be built connecting the boundary line between Canada and the United States with the Yukon. What progress has been made? Something may have been done which it is believed should be kept as a military secret; but if that is so, why do we not have a secret sitting to explain the whole matter to members who are eager for the information.
Besides that, we are not so sure that the enemy will invade this country along the coast; he may decide to invade this side of the Rockies, and Edmonton may be exposed. We know nothing about that, but we shall protect ourselves by having good roads which will facilitate communications and the transport of troops, munitions and supplies from one point to another in Canada, and between points in Canada and the United States. Those are things which could be done easily.
How much would it cost? Here we have a bill providing for the expenditure of two billions of dollars. I understand that it includes all expenditures for the army, navy and air force, and for some work of civilian departments. Certainly the building of good1 roads should be one of the first things done. It was done by the Romans two thousand years ago in Great Britain, and in many places those roads still exist. We see in England roads cemented by Caesar's men, and they have defied the centuries. We want roads in Canada which will afford the greatest opportunity of movement to Canadian troops, and give them the best possible chance to defend this country.
My second point in connection with the Department of Labour is this. The minister is a union man, and I regret to have to say to him that I have been disappointed with the unions. I will ask him to corroborate what I have to say. It is unfortunate, but the fact is that quite often the leader of a union represents himself, his immediate associates, his relatives and friends rather than the general membership. I have known of cases in the Canadian National Railways where the men did not get the support they expected from the leaders of the brotherhoods. I say that without any rancour; I say it just to put my case before this committee. I am just representing my electors. Quite often when a man gets to the top of the brotherhood he does not seem to be the same as when he was taking his first step upwards. It is difficult for the men to lodge complaints with

War Appropriation
the department when they cannot secure the approval of the head of their union. That is why they come to the members of parliament. They explain their cases in all confidence and ask us to defend them on the floor of the House of Commons. I hope the minister will be able to do something along the lines that have been suggested.
The Department of Transport has to do with the Canadian National Railways. I do not want to see an amalgamation of our railways because competition is necessary in this country. I would fear an exploitation by gangsters in an effort to make money by an undue increase in the price of the stocks of either one of the railway companies. I want competition, but I also want fair play for the men. I want a complete exposure of what has happened in connection with the financial structure of both railways.
I should like to say a word about the Department of External Affairs. Most of the agitation that has taken place with regard to Free France has been coming from civil servants. They are canvassing this one and that one and using intrigue in an effort to cause trouble in this country. I suggest that instructions should be given by each of the ministers that civil servants should mind their own business, especially in connection with external relations.

speechtext: The hon. member has spoken for forty minutes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think everyone in this house and in this country will get comfort from the fact that on May 1 the number of unemployed registered at the Enployment Service of Canada was the lowest in the history of the dominion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It should be.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. I would say to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) that I have knowledge of vacancies for 4,000 men who could be put to work tomorrow in his own province. The unemployed figure is 26,000, which includes men and women. Many of those are in and out of employment. You often run across that class of person in the country, a very necessary class of persons who are willing to undertake what might be termed casual work. In our search for manpower, order in council P.C. 1445 was passed on Alay 1. This provides for the registration of everybody between the ages of sixteen and seventy years who is out of employment. We want to know those people who want to work and those who do not want to work.
I consider we have the most efficient employment service in the history of this dominion. What we are trying to do is to make it a living thing, something that will render service not only to the employee but to the employer. I hope, when this period of stress is over, we shall have an employment exchange in the truest sense of the word, an exchange where men and women can be placed in close contact with work irrespective of where that work may be. Where necessary, we have paid the railroad fares of those persons who we considered were necessary to the war industry of Canada.
Some mention has been made of the labour union officials. I have had some knowledge of the officials of the labour unions of this dominion, and I think they compare favour ably with those in any other country in the world, and that covers a lot of territory. I believe this is exemplified by the situation that exists to-day in connection with strikes. At the moment there are 238 persons in Canada who are on strike. I do not think any country in the united nations, or probably in the dictator nations, can show a record like that. One strike is at a coca-cola plant, but I think we can get along without coca-cola. No one will suffer except people who are on a diet who drink a bottle of coca-cola and smoke a cigarette for lunch. Our future generations are likely to suffer because of that kind of thing. Then there is a window-cleaners' strike in Montreal, involving six people. We can get along without windows if necessary. Where the blitz is in operation in Europe, particularly in Germany, I imagine they are getting along without windows. Then there is a small strike at the Canadian Bridge company, involving twelve people. If my information is correct, these twelve men quit work to go somewhere else to work. All this I think demonstrates the good work being done by the trades union leaders and employers in this country. All parties in this parliament and the public in general should be encouraged by reason of that state of affairs. It is something of which we should be proud. I trust I have answered some of the questions raised by my hon. friend.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
Minister of Labour a question which I think has something to do with our war effort. It has bothered me for some time, especially when I hear and see the ability of hon. members to represent just causes in this house. Some of us were privileged to visit the magnificent plant in Montreal of the Canadian Car and Foundry company. We were interested in what they w.ere turning put, but I must admit that I was more interested in the men and women who toiled there than I was
War Appropriation

in the output. Repeatedly I asked how much the men were being paid, and I found that they were receiving the same rate of wages as was paid at the head of the lakes less the higher cost of living there.
I found, too, that in aeroplane works all across Canada wages were pretty much on the same level, but it was forcibly brought home to me when I was at home during the Easter holidays that persons engaged in the pulp and paper industry are paid much higher hourly wages at the head of the lakes than for similar work in the province of Quebec. I know the cost of living is higher at the head of the lakes because perhaps the food is better and of a higher quality, but a man who does a job has a right to the same rate of wages wherever the job may be done. The minimum wage in the union at the head of the lakes is about 57 cents an hour. In, the province of Quebec the rate is very much lower. This makes for unrest among the workers of Quebec and among the manufacturers of pulp and paper in other places. That is perhaps the reason why at the head of the lakes there is more lay-off than in paper mills in the province of Quebec. I would ask the Minister of Labour whether it would not be possible through the cooperation of the provinces to have a uniform scale of wages applicable to every industry throughout the length and breadth of this dominion. I think that wmuld make for a more united Canada. I understand that an administrator is to be appointed for the pulp and paper industry, and I am sure that a uniform rate of wages is one of the things that he will take up. I am sure the hon. member for Temiscouata would say that an employee in the province of Quebec should have the same rate of wages as an employee in the city of Fort William. I am sure he would say that the French Canadian can do as big a day's work as a man anywhere else, and I say to the members from the province of Quebec that this is one of the outstanding problems they must face in the future, namely, a standard wage level throughout the length and breadth of Canada, for a man is a man no matter where his employment may be.
Moreover, I think a lady, because she is a lady whether she toils or not, who does the same kind of work as a man should receive the same wage as a man. Here is one place where man should step down and recognize the ability of woman to work as well as he can. That is seen in this House of Commons where the lady members rival the best of men.

speechtext: The minister has been talking about strikes. It is not only strikes that interrupt work. There is sickness. A good doctor can tell at a glance whether a man or woman is sick or whether there is anything wrong. If he sees somebody needing attention he will say to him: "You go into the office." One doctor I know has three plants to look after in this way, and he has other doctors to help him. By this method these plants have cut their lay-offs by more than one half. Would the minister take something like that under consideration?

-he would be amazed at the strides which have been taken in that direction during the last generation. This dominion takes second place to no other

speechtext:
The Minister of Labour is surely familiar with the road policy of the dominion government during these past years. For a time grants were made under the Minister of Railways and Canals. At that time the Department of Railways and Canals were building parts of roads with subsidies which were spent under that department; afterwards the Department of Labour was associated with the provinces and the municipalities in the building and upkeeping of roads; and finally the contributions were sent by the Department of Labour to the provinces for certain particular roads which were described in the requests from the provinces. Afterwards roads and parts of roads were built by the Department of Mines and Resources and the Department of Public Works. But that was
War Appropriation

done before the war. Since the war started, I do not know of any roads that have been built by this government. I draw the minister's attention to the fact that the money spent for the trans-Canada highway has been much greater in Ontario than in the province of Quebec. In Ontario the expenditure for that purpose was S14,000,000, while in Quebec it was only about $400,000.
That being said, I ask the minister if it is not the policy of the government to build good military roads in this country, particularly between the shores of the St. Lawrence river and the boundary line of the United States. There are three highways there: the King Edward highway, which perhaps is now called the Laurier highway, between Rouse's Point and Montreal; the Levis-Jackman highway; and also the Riviere du Loup highway, which is a section of route No. 2, trans-Canada highway, and an old military route which was rebuilt at the time of the Fenian war. Work on this road, particularly because of our close relations with the United States, should be expedited. In fact it is now used by the army, in spite of some curves which should be reduced; and the pavement of that section of No. 2 highway should be put in the best possible condition. I ask the minister whether the government is not disposed to proceed with this work at the earliest available opportunity, so as to provide the greatest possible mobility for our troops in the event of an attack in that part of the country.

speechtext: I know that the clause has been carried, but I would ask the minister to be kind enough to say whether it is the policy of the government or not. If it is, I will congratulate them; if it is not, I shall continue my efforts to try to get them to do something.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: As my hon. friend, no doubt, well knows, the federal government stopped contributing to relief roads last year, and I understand that any roads which are now being built are built at the instigation of the Department of National Defence and for military purposes.
