subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I thank the minister for his answer, .and I will ask him if the Department of National Defence has adopted the policy of building roads required for military purposes. That is what I want to elucidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The only one that I remember is the Terrace-Prince Rupert highway, but there may be others. These are important defence projects for specific purposes, and if there is no other way to get the roads built, the dominion government does it as a matter of defence. Like my colleague, the Minister of Labour, however, I do not pretend to keep these projects in my mind; it is within the realm of another department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: May I call the minister's attention to another road coming within that category, to which I think the government should give attention. It is on the east coast, between Bathurst and the Miramichi river, commonly known as the Bathurst road, which would be an important road if it were necessary to remove any body of troops quickly along that area. I know there have been negotiations between the Department of National Defence and the province of New Brunswick. The province simply will not surface that road. I suggest that this ought to be called again to the attention of the Minister of National Defence with a view to reviewing the position.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I agree with what the leader of the opposition has said. It is a vital problem. We cannot insist too much upon it. Look at the size of this country. In the east there are only three railway lines; the transcontinental ; the Canadian Pacific Railway, which passes through United States territory for a certain distance; and the Intercolonial. If a bridge is blown up, the traffic stops; and it is necessary not only to protect bridges but also to improve the highways to provide against any deficiency with regard to railway traffic. At the present time railway traffic, both passenger and freight, is jammed, and of course the roads are most necessary for transportation by truck and car. Many military convoys pass over the route I have already mentioned.
I admit that the Prince Rupert highway or the British Columbia-Yukon highway may be very important. I do not discuss it at all; I agree with it. It is not, however, the only highway that is necessary in Canada from a military point of view; there are many others. They are the more necessary because we have not as many railways as have other countries, for the reason that our population is more scattered. Therefore it is most important to do that highway work at the earliest possible opportunity. Whether it is done by the Department of National Defence or the Department of Public Works or the Department of Labour or any other department does not matter, provided it is done. It should

War Appropriation
be done in case of emergency, or in case of any bridge being blown up and the traffic being blocked at any point. Under present circumstances it is most urgent to have it done. For instance, what would happen if the bridges on the Miramichi were blown up, if the bridge near Moncton where the transcontinental joins the intercolonial were blown up. Anything might happen. I do not need to say more; the maps and the timetables are there, and hon. members know the geography of our country. It is one of the most urgent things to be done, independently of any party consideration. It is vital to cut red tape at this point.
There are some guards, most of them returned men, on bridges; all right, give the returned men a chance; but the guards should be able-bodied men, familiar with handling a gun, to protect those vital arteries, the railways and highways. We cannot do too much in order to have that work done just as soon as possible, the same as it is done in any other country that is preparing itself for defence. I am told that the preparation has started. It is the very best thing to do, not only in the view of military experts but for the purpose of giving security to the population.
It is also very important to decentralize industry, particularly with regard to the railways. If a bridge is blown up and locomotives cannot cross to the shops where they are repaired or rebuilt, is it not vital that there shall be the largest number of shops available for urgent repairs in such cases? At the present time the policy of the Canadian National Railways is wrong in that respect. It is a policy of centralization at five or six points in Canada, to the detriment of smaller places. For instance, centralization is going on at Moncton, Montreal, Point St. Charles; at Stratford in Ontario; at Transcona near Winnipeg, and so on. At Riviere du Loup there are very fine shops. There is an erecting shop, one of the six or seven mechanical erecting shops, and there is a roundhouse. They can repair locomotives very well, and they do excellent work. At present many men there are laid off because there is not enough work, while at the same time at Moncton they cannot do all the work they have, and from Montreal they send their locomotives to Transcona for repairs. Think of the mileage cost. One must come down to common sense and not forget that what is done in smaller centres is probably more important than what is done in large centres.
I insist again on that policy of military roads, arteries. For commerce they may be used incidentally; after the war they may be 44561-202
used for tourist traffic, but now they are essential from the military point of view. I hope that the government will consider the matter, and that what I have said has not fallen on deaf ears.
Mr. O'BRIEN:	Earlier in the day the
hon. member for Parry Sound and the leader of the opposition, speaking of the defence of Halifax, brought to my mind' the situation just mentioned by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I wanted to refer to the matter at that time but the opportunity was not available.
The Miramichi river in my constituency, is one of the largest rivers in eastern Canada, having direct access to the sea. Some thirty miles from the sea we have a depth of water as much as forty-five feet. It is my belief that because of the knowledge the Germans have of that part of the country, from information gathered during their two or three years there carrying on shipping, they know every foot of ground probably much better than those of us who live in that community. For that reason I believe it is a strategic point in the defences of the eastern coast, particularly of Halifax.
The Canadian National railway crosses the two large branches of the Miramichi over very heavy steel bridges; and while we often hear the saying, "It can't happen here," it would not surprise me if any morning we learned that a submarine had come into the Miramichi and proceeded to damage or blow up these bridges. If that happened, Halifax would eventually starve to death, because the main line of the railway from upper Canada through Halifax to Great Britain would be cut. Halifax is reasonably well defended except for lack of the barrage balloons which the hon. member for Parry Sound mentioned and which I think is a worth-while recommendation. But it seems to me that if any attempt were made to damage Halifax, it could be readily done through the Miramichi. Some time ago I wrote to the Minister of National Defence pointing this out. I believe it is a most important and critical point in the defences of eastern Canada, and at present there is no protection whatever. A reasonably small net across the mouth of the Miramichi bay would, I think, afford adequate protection against the danger which I foresee, but which I very much hope may not happen.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is a question I should like to ask the Minister of Finance. Earlier in the session I addressed my question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but he quite properly stated it was a matter for the Minister of Finance to decide. Farmers in western Canada, while not criticizing the policy

War Appropriation

of maintaining price control, do feel critical of the government for having established a price ceiling without first establishing parity
of prices. The Searle Grain company in their letter of May 20 last established that fact quite well. They show that the present price of wheat is now 43 per cent below the 1913-14 parity price, and the 90 cent price established for the new crop is 31 per cent below parity. The price of hogs is now 14 per cent below parity, and steers 10 per cent below, but I understand the latter has now been adjusted. In any event this shows clearly that as far as agricultural products are concerned parity of prices has not been established.
It is interesting to note that when the matter was raised in the house the Minister of Agriculture stated: "We are taking every last dollar out of the treasury of Canada to deal with these problems which we feel it is safe to take at the present time." I do not think anyone would suggest that by this statement the minister meant that there was no more money available to the government wherewith they could pay a parity price to agriculture. I take it what the minister meant and what the Minister of Finance would mean is that if the government were to increase the price of agricultural products, they would thereby increase the purchasing power of the farmers, which would increase the demand for goods, and the result would be inflationary. I take it that this is really what the Minister of Agriculture was referring to at that time. 1 noticed a statement made by Mr. Donald Gordon some time ago in Winnipeg, and quoted in The Western Producer of April 23, as follows:
I do not want to leave the impression that in this question of the farmers relation to the price ceiling I dismiss the farmer's case and say: Take it or leave it.
Then he goes on:
What I do say is that if the price-ceiling policy is going to be successful it cannot be subject to qualification. Increases in agricultural prices would start the inflationary spiral in motion again . . . and the farmer has as much to lose as anyone in that event.
First of all he states that it is not a question of saying that the farmers must either take it or leave it, but later on he says that if prices of agricultural products were increased, the result would be inflation, and that, therefore, such increases cannot be allowed. I have a suggestion to offer to the Minister of Finance. Surely that difficulty could be overcome if the government would make up the difference between the parity price and the present price the farmers are receiving by a payment in the form of a certificate that could not be cashed until so many months after the end of the war.

That would absolutely obviate the danger of inflation and at the same time make it possible for the farmer to establish a sinking fund for the purpose of paying his debts at the end of the war. I wonder if the minister could explain why such a policy could not be adopted. I think he will have to admit that it would avoid any danger of inflation, so long as these certificates could not be cashed until after the war, and at the same time it would guarantee the farmer a parity price and put him on the same level as other industries.

The hon. gentleman has asked what would be the disadvantage in issuing war savings certificates to a number of people, I presume a large number of people, in this country. The disadvantage would be the great increase which would result in the national debt, and which we try to avoid if we possibly can. With regard to the question of parity in farm prices, surely we have debated that over and over again. I personally have made several speeches about it both inside and outside the house; and when I have been in this chamber while my colleague the Minister of Agriculture was addressing the house, I have been made very conscious of the fact that the debate on agricultural prices was going on not only hour after hour but day after day. I would respectfully suggest that after the tremendous length of time we have been on this bill, after having discussed the resolution for a great number of weeks and taken up these very questions, we should try to conclude the discussion to-night without opening up these matters all over again.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Before we finish with the Minister of Labour there is just one matter I should like to bring to his attention, which I am sure he can deal with very quickly. It is a matter which is causing a good deal of concern, and it is of some urgency. I refer to the question of the children of married

War Appropriation
women employed in war industries, which I understand comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour.
The extent of this problem may not be fully recognized by the house or by the country, though it is beginning to receive some attention in the press. In Montreal, in one plant alone, it is said there are employed 1,717 married women with children. In another plant it is said that of the 2,100 employees, 25 per cent are married women, while in a third plant out of 1,300 employees, 27 per cent are married women. In Montreal there are only three institutions equipped and qualified to look after the children of married women who go out to work. In Toronto a survey was conducted of five schools, and it was found that the mothers of 25 per cent of the children were out working, principally in war industries; and it has been stated in one magazine that 20 per cent of the children attending school have their mothers out at work. In Toronto there are only seven institutions equipped to look after these children. The facilities are hopelessly inadequate, and a single agency is said to have turned away 1,500 mothers who wanted to place their children regularly with it. I have no doubt that the same problem exists in other cities throughout Canada, such as Hamilton, Oshawa, Peterborough and so forth.
We can easily see what this leads to. In the first place it leads to malnutrition, and already there are alarming reports of increases in infant mortality in Ontario. It leads to truancy from school. It leads to a considerable increase in juvenile delinquency, an increase estimated at as much as from 50 to 100 per cent in the ages from eight to twelve. If we want married women working in war industries-and I think we do-then we need to look after them and their children, and this is a responsibility of the federal government, which is responsible for carrying on the war and providing the munitions necessary for that purpose. On the other hand, the problem is a complicated one, by reason of our relations with the provinces. Speaking in this house on March 24 of this year the Prime Minister said, as appears at page 1565 of Hansard:
The series of measures being undertaken to bring women into industries include:
6. The provision of nurseries and other means of caring for children.
Since then I understand the Minister of Labour has had this matter under consideration, but there is a great deal of concern being felt, and I think it would be exceedingly 44561-202 J
useful if at this time he gave a short statement indicating that the problem is being-attended to and that a solution will soon be found. It seems to me, if I may offer the suggestion, that three measures should be undertaken in this connection. First there is the problem of the children below school age, who do not go to school because they are too young. For them day nurseries should be provided near their homes, to take children in groups of fifty or sixty. These might be conducted in unoccupied schools, churches or other buildings, and trained personnel would have to be provided to look after these children. Then there are the children of school age, and that problem is becoming particularly important now that the summer is coming on. In this connection I suggest that the recreational facilities of the schools be made available during the summer months, so that the children may not be turned loose on the streets. This would continue the advantages of school life during the summer, and that is why this matter has become urgent. Then there is the whole question of the utilization of married women in war industries, and in this connection I suggest that we might well follow the practice which has been adopted in Britain; that is, as far as humanly possible limiting the employment of married women in war industries to employment on the day shifts.
This matter has already received some attention in Ontario, where there was passed,. I think at the last session of the legislature, a statute providing for cooperation. The matter has received attention in the province of Quebec, where Hon. Edgar Rochette, provincial minister of labour, had an exchange of correspondence with various trade unions^ and labour organizations. It has also received' attention in the press. In view of the urgency of the question and the concern that is felt, I think it would be interesting to learn from the minister what is being done in this connection.

speechtext:
My hon. friend and I have discusesd this matter before. Hon., members may rest assured that it is receiving, the earnest consideration of the Department of Labour. As the hon. member has indicated, the question comes under the jurisdiction of the director of selective service. What we have in mind is setting up standards and, if necessary, making some contribution to the establishment of these important services, if women are to go into war industries on the scale that we anticipate may be required in the not too distant future. I think he will probably agree with me it will be far better

first of all to start off in the large metropolitan centres, where they have had some experience in this regard. I agree with him that in a measure it falls within the jurisdiction of the provincial government, municipal organizations and voluntary organizations which have taken a great interest in this important function in connection with our war effort. He can rest assured that the agency under the director of selective service has a deep appreciation of the necessity for protecting the children about whom he has spoken so eloquently this evening. I believe the committee may safely leave this matter with the Department of Labour, particularly to the selective service branch, and rest assured that every move will be made with expedition to see to it that these good people are protected.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That, of course, is a reassuring statement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is intended to be.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes; it is intended to say, "We are going to do very well; leave us alone." What plan has been devised, if any, or are they just thinking about it? I was in a plant on Saturday which engages several thousand women working in three different shifts. Among them are a great many married women. Many of those married women work at night, and they travel long distances to get to their work. On that lovely June afternoon I just wondered to myself where their children were. More than that, as I watched them changing shifts I wondered to myself what was going to become of those people after the plant finished operation. That matter was discussed among ourselves. Those of us from the smaller provinces may not appreciate the full magnitude of the problem. A woman has to go out to work by the day, possibly, and somebody looks after her children. But here is a case where thousands are in these munitions plants, and there must be many hundreds of children who are not being looked after. It is not enough to say, "Oh, just leave it to us; we are thinking about it and talking about it." That is not quite good enough.
Having given this admonition to the minister, I shall ask the Minister of Finance a question which, I hope, will help us to get this measure through. If anyone examines the bill he will observe there is a new provision in it this year. I try to analyse these measures as they come along, in the light of past experience, and I now call attention to the fact that subsection 2, of section 3 is new. I believe I am correct in that.

Any expenditure required to be made by the government of Canada under any contract for munitions of war and supplies entered into by the government of Canada for the purpose of enabling any company wholly owned by the government of Canada to fulfil its obligations in respect of orders received by such company from the government of any British or foreign country allied with his majesty may be paid out of any unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund.
I assume the procedure set up in connection with these wholly owned government companies, partly owned government companies or companies partly owmed by this government and partly by the British government is that they have to be financed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is no question about that. So far as I know they are doing good work. Some of the best brains in the country are operating them; I believe I may pay that tribute. They are operating them in some instances at a dollar a year. I know the head of one of these companies, and he is working like a galley slave for this government for a dollar a year, without even any expenses. I do not think any of his own companies are getting any government contracts, either. It would seem, therefore, that he is the perfect dollar-a-year man. I had not intended to eulogize him, and I shall not mention his name. But I should like to know what control parliament has over these moneys?
This has introduced a new principle. We vote money, but what responsibility is there to parliament? That may be a purely academic question, but this is public money which has been taxed or borrowed from the people of Canada, and I should like to know what reports we have from any of these companies. Does this information appear in the auditor general's report? Do we learn in that report how the money is spent?
I will not go over the whole gamut of the operation of these companies, but I would ask the minister whether or not a principle is at stake. This is public money-and I say this, always keeping in mind the hon. member for Temiscouata, because what I say may serve as a text for another speech from the hon. member. I hesitate very much providing him with that; perhaps he does not need it.
However, I have been thinking about this matter ever since the announcement respecting the establishment of these wholly owned

War Appropriation
government corporations. Some huge corporations have been set up under this plan. Canadian Car Munitions Limited is a plant in connection with which $18,000,000 have been spent, and they are operating on what might be described as a fee basis. From what I can judge, I believe it is a well operated plant. I have great confidence in the management of it, and they are doing wonderful work for the country. But that is not the point I have in mind. What control has parliament over the operation of that kind of plant? I am sure the minister will say there is adequate treasury control, and I would be astonished if there were not. In fact, I take it for granted that the treasury are looking after the operation of that plant, and endeavouring to see that the government get adequate returns for the moneys expended, not only in connection with capital expenditures, which were made hurriedly and quickly, owing to pressure, but also in connection with the operation of the plant.
I suggest to the minister that a principle is involved which should be explained to the Canadian people. How are these companies to be made accountable to parliament? Are these to be ordinary government expenditures, or are we just to let the matter go? I do not know whether I have put the matter very well, because my ideas have not been well crystallized. I have made no inquiries; I suppose, had I called up some of the officers in the Department of Finance, they would have made an explanation. But I think this is the place where the explanation should be made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We would not have had the explanation if it had been sought privately.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is so. I suggest that it should be made here so that the public and the membership of this committee will understand the position. Here is a situation involving many millions of dollars not only in capital but also in operational costs.

speechtext: These crown companies are not comparable with the Canadian National Railways, for example, which has a separate set of auditors, and which is separate from the government. These companies are financed just as if they were government departments or branches.

Two or three companies

There is exactly the same

not know exactly the stage, but the comptroller of the treasury keeps very closely in touch with them, because frequently he speaks to me about some of the expenditures being made. They are also subject to audit by the auditor general.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
A few moments ago reference
was made to providing for the children of mothers who might be working in industry. There are a number of parasites in Canada at the present time who could be put to work before homes are broken up. The war has already broken up sufficient homes without any more being broken up unnecessarily. If the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) wants to know one instance, I can give him one to which reference has been made on several occasions.
I have particular reference to a gambling den which is authorized and legalized by this government and by other governments in the past. I understand there are thousands of *employees in this den who are paid at the expense, directly or indirectly, of the farmers of western Canada. These farmers are now asked to go without the cost of production of a number of their products. If anyone should make a mistake as to the organization to which I have reference, it is the Winnipeg grain [DOT]exchange. On different occasions we have tried to have this exchange closed and have pointed
{Mr. Ilsley.)
out that the grain exchange in the old country was closed at the beginning of the war. Some of us are convinced that the government of the old country would be quite satisfied to have the exchange here closed if some of our friends in the government were willing. Apparently that is not the situation. Before any more homes are broken up, I would suggest that all the parasites in this gambling den in Winnipeg be put to work in some profitable manner. Let them get out and make an honest living for a change.
A short while ago the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) asked the Minister of Finance about the payment of parity prices for farm products and outlined the method by which that could be done. Because there was some sense to the question the minister immediately wanted to close off the debate and get this bill through. Some of my hon. friends to my right have suggested on two or three occasions that the debate has gone on long enough and should be closed, but some of us who want to say a few words find that we cannot because they are still talking, in a number of instances, nonsense. The Minister of Finance said that it would increase the national debt, but I ask him if the national debt is not being increased in order to pay several manufacturers of war commodities far in excess of that to which they are entitled. I have no objection to their receiving the cost of production plus a reasonable profit, but I cannot see why they should be paid exorbitant profits when growers of food are asked to go without their cost of production.
Before sitting down-I may have quite a time having an opportunity to speak again because it took me a long time to get the floor on this occasion-I should like to say that I support the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) in his remarks about labour. I believe something should be done, and done in a hurry, along that line. It has been suggested that farm help be trained, but I want to say that help cannot be trained in a week or two, or a month or two, to do the work that must be done on a farm to-day. Tractors, in some instances costing as much as S2.500, binders and other machines are used, and they might not be operated efficiently by someone who has lived in a city or town all his life. Some of them might act like the city man on the farm who was sent out one morning to put the harness on a horse. When the farmer went out later he found this man had put the harness on a milch cow. Because the cow happened to have horns, the so-called farmhand found it impossible to get the collar on. I think a lot of damage would be done, I admit not intentionally, by using untrained labour.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to follow the text that has been indicated to me by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. At times he makes a good speech. He makes a good speech when he accompanies it with a broad smile. Then he is himself. To-night he spoke very well, and so did my hon. friend the member for Weyburn and the Minister of Finance.
It is easy to come to an understanding; but what the government must not forget is this, that centralization does not come from the ministers but comes from underneath. It comes from those in the civil service-call them civil servants or officials, it is of no importance-who are greedy for power. It is in virtue of this principle of centralization that men are paid, not according to their worth, but according to the size of their staff. The more staff they have, the more important they are; the more power they have, and the bigger the salary they get. That is the reason why we have centralization in Ottawa. It is just because of the greed of high officials who want to become more and more powerful, at the expense of old-established traditions and rights, at the expense of the constitution, and perhaps at the expense of unity in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No; it is not carried, and the more "carried" is said, the less likely the section is to carry. I am not here to cause obstruction. I am here to express my views and deep convictions. We have heard a great deal about unity in this country, and the conclusion of what was said was that the province of Quebec was a reserve and that the people of that province were entirely different from the people of the rest of Canada. We have had sermons on unity which gave the impression that we are asking the majority in this country to be lenient and kind toward
the minority of the province of Quebec. That is not the way for us to deal together as free citizens in this great land. No, sir. We both, English-speaking and French-speaking, have our qualities and our defects, but we must come together just as we are to try to solve our problems. How can that be done? It can be done if we have the truth about the French-Canadian war effort. We do not have it. I wrote to the minister on January 14, asking his help in securing some information about French Canadians who had enlisted in English-speaking Canadian units. I had received no answer by March. Then I put the letter on Hansard. Still I had no answer. I sent a copy of Hansard to the hon. gentleman concerned, accompanied by another letter. Still no answer. Afterwards I met his secretary, who showed me a letter that had been signed three weeks before by the minister, and that letter was not handed to me because it was not permitted by the Department of National Defence and other departments. Then I wrote another letter. The secretary of the minister telephoned me that the minister had put a note on my letter saying that according to him I was perfectly right in asking for that information. But I have not yet received an acknowledgment of my first letter. Is that reasonable?
What I want are the complete figures about the French-Canadian war effort. When we have them we shall be able to discuss the matter with anyone. If we are wrong, so much the worse for us; if we are right, so much the better for us. We shall not be afraid to tell the truth, and we shall not be influenced by anV propaganda published by those who have a personal interest in slandering the province of Quebec.
I want to defend my own people because they are worthy of being defended. I have the utmost respect for the farmers, the sailors, the airmen and the soldiers and all the citizens of my province, who are equal to anybody in this country. We must not be considered a reserve in the province of Quebec. That is most insulting. We want to be treated exactly as others are treated. We do not want any unfairness or injustice. We want to be treated fairly and squarely.
Some people speak on our behalf. They have no right to do it because when they speak they do not think of the common people, and they do not interpret the views of the common people. They express views that are not ours, and it is for their own selfish purposes that they do that.
In this war effort the people of the province of Quebec cannot be ignored. There
War Appropriation

must be a complete knowledge of what has happened in the past so that we can be fair in judging the present and the future. Let us have the figures. How is it that we cannot get them? How is it that they are not accessible to all members of parliament and to all citizens of this dominion? That information would mean more for national unity than any eloquent speeches uttered by gifted speakers in this country, or speeches delivered by some one but written by others. It is time that we speak face to face, say what we have to say, and not be afraid of any kind of propaganda. The most disastrous propaganda was that used in the last plebiscite campaign in which all those who were not seeing eye-to-eye with the government were branded as traitors. Even in this chamber there were members who were making the worst insinuations against their colleagues who did not see eye-to-eye with their views, however absurd they were.
I hope, sir, that in the future, the errors of the past will not be repeated; that a broad outlook will be taken, and that all Canadians, whether English-speaking or French-speaking, will understand that this is our common country; that we are all in the same boat and that we have an interest in coming closer together for a common purpose. Let us not make anyone out worse than he is. Let not any French Canadian think the Englishspeaking Canadian is otherwise than he is, and let not the reverse occur either. There are no angels in this country. There are guardian angels over every citizen, but they are invisible. Those we see are not angels, although they may be very good citizens.
Is it not possible, sir, to come back to the love and defence and protection of our land? I have been advocating it. If this argument is not accepted, let us try another one with those who are not Canadians at heart, with those who are imperialists. Let us say to them: "We want immediately the roads that are necessary for the war effort. If you will not build them for the defence of this country, build them at least for the transportation of supplies to Great Britain and our friendly allies overseas." H the defence of our country is not enough in the eyes of those who do not consider Canada worth defending, let us use the other argument and ask that roads be built for the transportation of supplies to Great Britain and our friendly allies. Let us also have mobile units for the defence of this country, not only trains but trucks for the transportation of our soldiers. We should have

automobiles, tanks and all the mobile equipment that is required for an army in a country the size of ours. These things should be provided.
Besides that, let us have in each branch of the Department of National Defence the direction in the hands of Canadians, not outsiders. We should have Canadians to decide the policy of this government. We should not be in the hands of outsiders. The reason why our defence is neglected is that everything is suggested by outsiders and is done on their advice. We want Canadians at heart, whether born in this country or not, but people who are to live in this country after the war is over, and who are not to go away like migratory birds.

Section agreed to.
Section 3 agreed to.
On Section 4-loans authorized.

This is the section under which we would naturally discuss the question of the financial policy of the government; but, in view of the fact that it is desired that we get through with this bill as rapidly as possible, I will defer the discussion to a later time.
The minister on several occasions has pointed out that the government's policy of taxation and of issuing bonds is to restrict the spending power of the public. We have asked why he does not make use of the services of the Bank of Canada, but he has never given a satisfactory answer to that question. At a later stage I shall be prepared to discuss the matter at some length and ask the minister to give a satisfactory explanation of why we are not using the Bank of Canada instead of the chartered banks. Since the declaration of war, we have borrowed directly or indirectly from the chartered banks close to one thousand million dollars-to be exact, I believe $950 million. We consider that when it is necessary to expand the amount of money in circulation, that should be done through the Bank of Canada and not through private moneyed institutions.

He asked me to prepare and put on record a statement of the borrowings by the dominion government and also those of the Canadian National Railways. I have a statement relating to the dominion government, and with the permission of the committee I will have it printed in the proceedings at this stage. This is the statement:
Particulars of the Issue of Dominion of Canada
Bonds Outstanding which are Payable in New York Funds
1.	Thirty-year 5 per cent bonds dated May 1,
1922, due May 1, 1952-$100,000,000.
This issue was sold in 1922 to provide cash for various general purposes of the government.
2.	Thirty-year 4 per cent bonds dated October 1,
1930, due October 1, I960-$100,000,000.
One hundred million dollars issued for cash in October, 1930, of which $25,000,000 was used for the redemption on April 1, 1931, of 5 per cent bonds dated April 1, 1916. This latter issue was part of a $75,000,000 loan issued for the refunding of maturing loans and general purposes.
3.	Ten-year 2J per cent bonds dated August 15,
1935, due August 15, 1945-$76,000,000.
The proceeds of this issue were used for the following purposes:
(a)	Redemption of $50,000,000 Dominion of Canada 2 per cent promissory notes dated September 1, 1934 and due September 1, 1935, which, in turn had been issued to redeem $50,000,000 of a $60,000,000 issue of fifteen months' notes on September 1, 1934. This latter issue had been sold on July 1, 1933, for the refunding of an issue of $60,000,000 dated October 1, 1932. The issue of $60,000,000 notes dated October 1, 1932, had been sold to provide cash to redeem in part $40,000,000 two-year 4 per cent notes dated December 1, 1930, and $13,000,000 treasury notes dated September 19, 1932, and maturing December 17, 1932. I would remind the committee that last spring I asked the Minister of Finance if he thought that Sir Edward Peacock would come to Canada, and he said no. Since then I have been asking a question as to the coming of Sir Edward Peacock to Montreal on June 25 when Sir Arthur Salter was also at the Ritz-Carlton, and I asked if any minister had met him. I know the Minister of Finance was not in town; he was in his own beautiful province at the moment, but Sir Edward Peacock was met by the Minister of Munitions and Supply and also by the Minister of National Defence in the capacity of Acting Minister of Finance. I thought the work of Minister of National
Defence was a full-time job, especially in view of the fact that the minister is seldom in his place here. I thought he was always veiy busy 'with his staff discussing the-problems of his department. So I was greatly surprised when I learned that he was Acting Minister of Finance and acting so precisely when Sir Edward Peacock and Sir Arthur Salter came to Montreal. Sir Edward Peacock is a director of the bank of Montreal and the Canadian Pacific Railway company and is the gentleman supposed to come to- America' to sell the stock of the Canadian Pacific. Whether or not he was successful in the United States I do not know, but I know he was successful with the Bank of Canada. If he did not sell the Canadian Pacific stock to the Bank of Canada, it is held there under guarantee awaiting the action of the government, probably awaiting the enactment of this bill, and we shall have amalgamation of railways under that.
The committee and the house know that I have always been opposed to amalgamation of the railways, opposed from the point of view of the public and also from the point of view of the employees of the railways. It has been the traditional policy of the Liberal party to oppose the amalgamation of the railways and to condemn the Tories just on account of their railway policy during the last war. If we are to have amalgamation by this government, what difference would there be between the Liberal party and the Conservative party?

Then, on March 23 I had a question on the order paper resulting from an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of March 21, stating that the armed Canadian forces were to use horses for transport. My idea at that time was that it would not handicap agriculture, because I believe people are using tractors as much as possible, and I thought this would be a market in which surplus horses could be disposed of. I understand publicity is carried on by the department in a number of ways. One is by the sending out of publications through mailing lists; another is through the press, where articles are sent to the press from time to time. Then there are exhibits at fairs. Is there any connection between the data accumulated by the Department of Agriculture and that accumulated by the bureau of statistics? Sometimes it is thought that the figures are not altogether reliable, and I should like to know whether there is any connection between the two branches, whether they collaborate in the gathering of data, and, if so, to what extent.
Then, what amount is spent on each class of publicity-that is, on exhibits at fairs, publications of articles in newspapers, and the like? How are mailing lists made up? Are they changed from year to year, or do they go on from one year to another? How are the newspapers, in which these articles are published.
IMr. Gardiner.]
chosen? Are they chosen all across the dominion, regardless of size, circulation or political leanings?

The first question has to do with the manner of gathering statistics. The bureau of statistics, which is connected with the Department of Trade and Commerce, does consult with officials of the Department of Agriculture in the gathering of material. They have a service, and we have a service which checks on the different markets. Sometimes there is a variation in the figures obtained.
Quite a serious one.

The figures put out by the bureau of statistics are sometimes based upon estimates gathered by certain methods, and by comparisons with conditions existing previously. Some of our statistics are gathered directly from the markets, through our inspectors on those markets. A correction takes place as between the two branches. But it is just possible that between the time statistics are gathered and the time the correction is made, some figures available to officers in the Department of Agriculture may differ from those given out by the bureau of statistics.
That holds good not only with respect to markets but also with respect to the number of cattle and hogs throughout the country.
Yes; it might apply to any of those things. But usually before anything is given out to the country, the figures are corrected as between the two departments, and conform as nearly as possible.
How are mailing lists made up, and how are the newspapers, in which these articles are published chosen?

Certain articles appear only in farm papers. My understanding is that those articles appear in all farm papers across Canada. There are other articles which appear only in local papers, and the method followed there is, I believe, to get in touch with the secretary of the association, and to deal with all papers of certain classifications across the country.
No attention is paid to political leanings or anything of that kind. As was mentioned a moment ago, papers of a certain classification are taken right across Canada. I presume that is based largely upon the subscription lists of the papers or the community that they serve. For other articles we use the daily press. It all depends upon the importance of the article and the necessity of getting it out in a short space of time. Articles that have

Supply-Agriculture-Publicity
to do with something that we want done within a week or two weeks would be of no value if published in a monthly agricultural paper, or possibly in a bi-weekly publication. In that case we would have to use the daily press in order to get the articles out to the public in time. Of course we supplement the publicity in the press with publicity over the radio and with information in pamphlet and other forms.
Does the department deal directly with the newspapers, or does it work through an advertising agency?
There is a press sheet made available weekly without any intermediary, but the advertising is done largely through the Canadian advertising agency with headquarters in Montreal.

That is correct.

Exhibits are quite often put
on at fall fairs, and I should like to know if it is intended to carry out this practice during this coming year. How are the fairs chosen? I have noticed bacon exhibits and other types of exhibits which are quite instructive. Are these fairs chosen on the basis of attendance, because they are class A or class B fairs, or is the selection made indiscriminately?

As hon. members know, during the last two years we have eliminated grants to fairs, and we have also limited our activities in connection with exhibits because of the cut made in the estimates. We follow the practice generally of having an exhibit in one zone in one year and then switching the exhibit in the following season. That makes it possible to have an exhibit shown generally throughout the country over a period of years. There will be some exhibits at class A fairs and there will be other exhibits at class B fairs; in each case, some of these fairs have ceased to operate during the war period. Generally speaking, we are carrying on the same activities as were carried on prior to the war, but at a lesser cost and in lesser volume.

I am interested in a fair which is neither class A nor class B, although it has a fairly good attendance. I have never understood how a board of directors or a secretary of a fair should go about getting an exhibit of this kind. I have been at fairs where these exhibits were shown, and they attracted a lot of attention. I think they are a good thing, and I should like to know how to go about making an application, particularly if a certain attendance is necessary before such application is considered.

It is not the practice to show exhibits at the smaller fairs, but that is done on occasion. Any fair board is at liberty to make application to the department for an exhibit, which application will be considered. It sometimes happens that an exhibit is being shown at a larger fair, and the necessary equipment can be moved to a smaller fair and the exhibit shown in about the same period of time. There are many details that enter into the matter.
What amounts are paid to the weekly, daily and monthly press?

Nothing is paid for the articles that go-out from the department, but we do pay for advertising. A certain sum is paid to the advertising agency for the publication of advertising matter in a certain classification of publication. The agency makes the arrangements with the different papers.
What sort of advertising?

It is largely war projects. We may want more hogs, and we advertise accordingly. We may want certain things done in connection with apples, or we may try to boost the sale of apples. In that case advertising is issued right across the country. It is advertising to increase the sale of farm products or the production of farm products.
What amount was paid by the agency to the weekly press in the provinces?

The amounts of which I have been speaking really come under the war appropriation vote which was discussed last week. I refer to the advertising of pork products and other things of that kind. I have not the information with me as to what was paid to the different papers.
Was that amount paid direct to the weekly newspaper association, which would divide it?
We indicate to the agency what we want done; a price is set, and the agency makes the distribution of the amounts.
What amounts were paid by the agency to the weekly and daily press?
I will bring the war estimates with me the next time I am before the committee and answer that question for the hon. member. I have only the general estimates before me.

This is an estimate of the department; it is not a war appropriation.

The money spent under this vote is largely to prepare the material that goes out to the press, for which we do not pay. Since the war we have cut advertising out of this vote, and it is now done under the war requirement.
Is all the advertising under this vote done in Canada, or is any done in Great Britain?

There is no advertising under this vote. This covers publicity in the form of pamphlets and so forth, material for which we do not pay. We send it out to the newspapers, and it may or may not be published, although most of it is.
What portion of the $109,650 voted last year has been expended?
There is no balance; it has all been spent.
How many publications are issued? Does the whole cost of printing, paper, and so forth come out of this vote?
The full cost does not come out of this vote. The cost of the staff that prepares the material comes out of this vote, but further down there is an item covering the printing and stationery.

I have often thought that the material which is being sent out by the department does not get enough publicity. By that I mean that a number of excellent pamphlets are issued by the department from time to time and kept in stock showing how different crops and different plants should be cultivated, soya beans, for example, and sometimes I think the public know little or nothing about these pamphlets being available. From the pamphlets the people would be able to learn how to produce these things, but do they know they are available? Is anything being done to acquaint the public with the fact that this great number of publications is available and that by asking for them the public can get them and study them with a view to producing to better advantage than perhaps they are doing at the present time?

All of the publications that go out from the department are reviewed in the press at the time they are published, and also reviewed over the radio. Then we have a long mailing list to which we send these publications. We try in every way to get the knowledge over to the public that the publications are in existence and can be had by people asking for them. A few of them have to be purchased. We do everything possible to make the public acquainted with the fact that the publications are available.

I think the hon. member for Haldimand has raised a very good point. The department prepares a great deal of free literature about which the people know little. I know that one year I secured a large quantity of different pamphlets on various subjects, poultry raising, hog feeding and so forth, and sent them out to rural schools in my constituency. The teachers put them on a desk where the children had access to them, and I was surprised how many people wrote in asking where they could secure copies. They had not known they were available. Many people do not get the newspapers, and those who do might not see the review. I do not know whether it would be possible to make these publications available to rural schools. That might be too large a territory to cover, but certainly the agricultural clubs should receive them and perhaps school teachers might be circularized and told that this material was available, and that if they had an agricultural club in their community the department would send them the literature. I know that people wTho have received this literature were grateful to get it, and we ought to make it known that these publications are available.

Some years ago I think the schools used to receive in the early fall a leaflet giving a list of the publications that could be applied for. I am thinking of twenty years ago. Has that practice been discontinued? I know I used to pick out a number of pamphlets from the list and send in for them. I can see the list in my mind's eye now. I do not know whether the list went out to all the schools, but I got one for several years.

There is such a list available to people who apply for it. I do not think it is customary to send it to all the schools, but it would be sent to a school if the teacher asked for it.
Perhaps I wrote in for the list in the beginning, and my name was continued on the mailing list.
Yes. People send in for the list and then select what pamphlets they wish.
Is the publication known as the "Agricultural Situation Outlook" still published?
It is not published in the form in which it was issued originally, but a monthly review is published.

In the early part of this session I made inquiries of the department with regard to this pamphlet which was issued for a number of years in peace time. I find among the farmers I represent quite a demand for the "Agricultural Situation Outlook". It was an informative publication covering several branches of agriculture and contained many interesting articles on the farm situation generally. I was wondering why the publication was discontinued unless there was some good reason for that.

The reason was the
expense of getting out a publication of that kind with our estimates cut down as they have been since the war started. I might add that it is much more difficult, I think the hon. member will agree, to publish such an outlook in war time than in peace time. The term "outlook" indicates the nature of a publication of that kind.

How is the mailing list
compiled and kept up to date?

It is a continuing list which has been built up over a long number of years, and we try to keep the list as up to date as we can. If you check the list tomorrow you might find the name of somebody on it who died last year, but even in that event the publication would not be wasted because there would no doubt be someone at that address who would get the mail. As close a check as possible is kept of the list, and names are struck off when persons have moved, but there is just the possibility that there may be some overlapping in a list of that kind.

I agree with the hon.
member for Haldimand that a great many of these publications are very useful. Last year I carried some home with me in my car, and I would slip them out to farmers.
One was on soya beans, I remember, and another on beef and how to select and cook it. I happened to leave one or two of these publications with a family in my town. Last week the Wolseley community war service organization put on a carnival, and this woman, who is one of the homemakers' group, wrote to me that they were conducting a booth at this carnival and asked if I would select a number of pamphlets such as I had left on this occasion, or any others, and send them to her. I selected eight or ten. One was entitled "Milk, the Perfect Food," and another was headed "Why Pasteurize Milk?" There were also two or three about canning and preserving fruits. I have received word that they went like hot cakes. The homemakers' group made over $100 at their booth. No doubt there will be a demand for some of these publications. I understand that the minister's department is putting out a pamphlet on how to can preserved fruits without sugar. I believe that if such a publication is intended, it would be a good thing to get a little publicity through the weekly press or advertise it in some way, because now that sugar is rationed it would be a fine thing to have this information in the hands of the people generally.

The only thing I can
say with regard to the matter is that our department has a service which is working out plans of that kind. Many women have been canning certain fruits and vegetables without the use of very much sugar; and all information with regard to that sort of thing is gathered together, put into the form of publications and sent out for the benefit of others. That work is going on constantly and I am sure, is helpful.

Does each agricultural
representative get a quantity of this literature, or how is it distributed?

Yes; they are all on
the mailing list and get quantities of it from time to time.
Could the minister give the committee any idea of the number of hours per week on the average occupied by Canadian Broadcasting Corporation broadcasts sponsored by the Department of Agriculture?

There is half an hour
every day in connection with giving market prices and that kind of thing. There is some time in addition, but I have not complete figures.

Is that sponsored by
the department, or is it Canadian Broadcasting Corporation activity?

These are Canadian
Broadcasting Corporation broadcasts. I hope the hon. member is not confusing it with the agricultural forum which was sponsored by the federal and provincial authorities.
No.

The department itself
does not actually sponsor the agricultural programme. We supply the material; that is the basis for it. In that sense maybe we are responsible for it. I would not like to say that we are sponsoring it.

From a practical point
of view, when the Department of Agriculture decides that it is in the interests of the farmers of the dominion that a broadcast should be made over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, is that initiated by the Department of Agriculture and, if it does, what is the practical means whereby the broadcast goes on the air? Does the Department of Agriculture go to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and ask for a date and for the particular length of time during which it wishes to broadcast? Does that come direct from the Department of Agriculture to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation?

Yes. Whenever any
special programme is put on, or we desire to have any special broadcast, we go to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and arrange for the person who is to broadcast, and so on.
Do you pay for it?

No, we are not
required to pay for it. Where it is in the national interest we are not required to pay.
Has the department paid for any programme over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the last year?

No, not from my
memory, excepting broadcasts which are put on in connection with a matter like our acreage reduction plan, advertising in the west. Some of that is paid for.
When you pay for it, do you place it through an advertising agency or direct through the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation?

The last arrangements, which were made-for example, for the putting on of the broadcasts with regard to acreage reduction last spring-were made through the J. J. Gibbons Company, whose office is at Regina. They made the arrangements for the radio, largely because they are the agency which does that kind of thing in that area.
Who paid the commission on the government advertising over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in connection with this particular matter?

That was not all over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It was over local stations, a combination of local stations. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation may have been in it as well, but much of it went over local stations.

But if that was a network programme it would be placed with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The point I am getting at is this. We were amazed this morning, in the radio committee, to find that the victory loan campaign and certain other campaigns were placed with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation through advertising agencies, and that commissions were paid to the advertising agencies for radio time obtained by the government for these national campaigns. Yet we have been told in this chamber that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is an agency of the crown. It seemed extraordinary, and I wondered if the Department of Agriculture were doing the same thing.
Mr. GARDINER; Ordinarily we go direct to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and make our arrangements direct with them. The only case I can recall, which is an exception, is the one I have mentioned. I am quite sure that that agency did make some arrangements for our advertising in the west. It was largely because we were making arrangements for the general advertising put out by that agency, and I am quite certain that they arranged for that broadcasting as well.

To hark back to the evidence which came out on the radio broadcasting commission: there is an interdepartmental committee headed by Mr. Justice Davis, deputy minister of national war services, a purely advisory committee, but one which apparently is working on the question of coordinating the matter of governmental official information which is to be relayed to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for dissemination throughout Canada. I was wondering whether the Department of Agriculture, before it initiates a broadcast over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, sends or has the informational scripts sent to the interdepartmental committee; whether arrangements are made direct with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself, or through the interdepartmental committee which was set up.

I think I am correct in stating that that organization is not yet func-

I hope that the minister is correct in what he says in this regard, because the evidence we have heard is not in entire agreement with his statement with respect to the setting up of the committee.
In what way?
